glossary.definition: Atomic, consistent, isolated and durable. A change happens completely, or not at all.
A common way to solve a problem that causes more problems later.
A change that lets old client code keep working with the new server.
A change to an API that makes existing client code stop working.
An organization that signs digital certificates, so browsers can check a website's identity.
The set of algorithms that client and server use for key agreement, authentication and encryption.
The way a server picks the best version of a resource for the client.
Data that proves who the user is, such as cookies or HTTP authentication.
A short value that names one version of a resource. It changes when the resource changes.
Waiting longer after each failed try before the next one, for example 1, 2, then 4 seconds.
The stable release of a feature, after its preview.
The first step of a TLS connection, where client and server agree on keys and settings.
A unique value the client sends with a request, so the server can spot a retry of it.
Sending the same request many times has the same intended effect on the server as sending it once.
A central service that signs users in and issues access tokens.
A signed JSON token with claims about a user, used for access control.
Many servers share the requests, but they look like one server to the client.
One client saves over another client's change, so the first change is lost.
An attacker who sits between the browser and the server, and reads or changes the traffic.
The browser guesses the MIME type by looking at the bytes of the file.
Sending many requests and responses at the same time over one connection.
Not meant to be read by the client. Only the server knows what it means.
The protocol, host and port of a URL together.
A condition that the server checks before it runs the request.
An OPTIONS request the browser sends first, to ask if the real request is allowed.
A limit on how many requests a client may send in a period of time.
The short, optional text after the status code, like Not Found, written for humans.
An HTTP method that only reads data and does not change the state of the server.
With the same meaning, even when some details differ.
A way for a server to send many small messages over one open HTTP response.
A series of requests that the server links to one user, often with a cookie.
A resource that exists only once, so there is no list of them.
A stateless protocol keeps no link between one request and the next.
A resource the client reads to see the progress of a long-running operation.
The messages a client and a server exchange to open a TCP connection.
A rate limit method where capacity refills all the time, up to a maximum.
The rightmost part of a domain name, for example com in example.com.
A short failure that often goes away when you try again.
Any tool that acts for the user, most often the web browser.
A universally unique identifier: a long ID, often random, so two values almost never match.

boss.title: Weekend 1 boss: the new checkout page

situation.text: A shop moves its checkout page to a new address, `checkout.shop.example`. The shop API stays at `api.shop.example`. On the first test day, three things go wrong:

items: The browser blocks every call from the checkout page to the API.
The login cookie does not reach the API.
A slow phone network makes some customers tap "Pay" twice. Two orders are created.

situation.text: You are the tech lead. Write a short design doc that fixes all three. A design doc is a short plan you write before you code. A Mermaid diagram is a drawing made from a few lines of text.

boss.mermaidStarter:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant API as api.shop.example
    Browser->>API: OPTIONS /orders (preflight)
    API-->>Browser: ??? (which headers?)
    Browser->>API: POST /orders
    API-->>Browser: ???
boss.coachPrompt: You are my tech lead coach. Below is my design doc for a made-up checkout problem. Do not give me a model answer yet. Ask me ONE question at a time about my options and my decision. Wait for my reply. Give hints, not solutions. After three rounds, tell me which trade-off I missed. Then ask me to explain the trade-off again in my own words. Show me two English mistakes and ask me to fix them.
boss.modelAnswer:
Read this only after the chat with the coach. Compare it with your own doc. Your answer can be different and still good. What matters is that you named the trade-offs. ## Problem The new checkout page and the API are on different origins. The browser blocks the calls, sends no login cookie, and a slow network creates double orders. We know it is fixed when a test customer can pay once, with one tap, and see one order. ## Options and decision | Problem | Options | Decision | |---|---|---| | 1. Browser blocks the calls | A: Serve the API under the checkout origin with a proxy. B: Add CORS headers on the API for `https://checkout.shop.example`. | B. The API opts in for one named origin. Source: [MDN: CORS](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS) | | 2. No login cookie | A: Send the token in a header instead of a cookie. B: Keep the cookie, set `credentials: "include"`, and answer `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. | B. It is the smallest change. The origin stays one name, never `*`. Source: [MDN: CORS, credentials](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS#requests_with_credentials) | | 3. Double orders | A: Disable the Pay button after one tap. B: Send an idempotency key with each payment. | Both. The button helps most people. Only the key makes a retry safe. Sources: [RFC 9110, 9.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-idempotent-methods), [Stripe](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests) | ## Trade-offs - A CORS rule for one origin is safe, but every new site needs a change on the API. - Cookies across origins need care. A wrong origin rule could let another site use the cookie. - An idempotency key means the API must store keys and their results. ## Risks - A typo in the allowed origin breaks checkout again. A test on the real address catches it. - A key that is reused for a different payment returns the old result. The client must make a new key per payment. ## Diagram ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Browser as checkout.shop.example participant API as api.shop.example Browser->>API: OPTIONS /orders (preflight) API-->>Browser: Allow-Origin: https://checkout.shop.example
Allow-Credentials: true Browser->>API: POST /orders + cookie + Idempotency-Key: k1 API-->>Browser: 201 order 42 Browser->>API: POST /orders again (slow network) + Idempotency-Key: k1 API-->>Browser: 201 order 42 (the same order, not a new one) ```

weekends.adrCoachPrompt: You are my tech lead coach. Below is an ADR I wrote for a real decision at work. Do not rewrite it for me. Ask me ONE question at a time about the context, the options I did not take, and the consequences. Wait for my reply. Give hints, not solutions. After three rounds, tell me which consequence I missed. Then ask me to explain the decision again in my own words. Show me two English mistakes and ask me to fix them.

intro.title: How a page reaches your browser
screens: HTTP is how a browser fetches a web page. The browser is the client, and it always sends the first message: a request. The server answers with a response.
One page needs many requests. The browser first fetches the HTML document. Then it fetches the scripts, the CSS and the images that the page uses.
Between the browser and the server there are often proxies. A proxy can keep a cache of answers, filter them, or share the load between several servers.
HTTP is sent over TCP, or over a TCP connection that TLS encrypts.
intro.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Proxy: Request
  Proxy->>Server: Request
  Server-->>Proxy: Response
  Proxy-->>Browser: Response

screens.text: HTTP is a client-server protocol. One side sends a request. The other side sends back a response. The side that sends the request is the client. It is usually your web browser.

The browser is always the one that begins a request. The server never begins one. Some mechanisms were added over the years to simulate messages that start at the server. But plain HTTP always starts at the client.
Example: you open the page developer.mozilla.org. The browser sends GET / HTTP/1.1 with the header Host: developer.mozilla.org. The server answers with HTTP/1.1 200 OK and the page.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Server: GET / HTTP/1.1
  Server-->>Browser: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

catch.question: In plain HTTP, which side sends the first message?
choices: The server, when it has new data
Whichever side opens the connection first
The proxy that sits between them
catch.explanation: HTTP is a client-server protocol. The client, usually the browser, always starts the request.

card.text: HTTP is a client-server protocol. The client sends a request, and the server sends back a response. The client is usually your web browser. The browser always starts the request. The server never starts it. Some mechanisms only make it look like the server started. Between the client and the server there can be proxies, for example caches or gateways.
card.example: You open https://example.com in your browser. The browser sends GET / HTTP/1.1 with the header Host: example.com. The server answers with HTTP/1.1 200 OK and the HTML page.

review.question: What can sit between the client and the server?
review.answer: Proxies, for example caches or gateways.

workedExample.problem: Your product manager wants the server to send a new price to an open product page. You only use plain HTTP.
steps: Remember the rule: in HTTP, the client always starts the request.
So the server cannot send the new price on its own.
The page must send a new request to get the new price.
workedExample.answer: Plain HTTP cannot push data to the page. Let the page send a new request for the fresh price.

tradeOff.situation: A manager changes a price while a customer has the product page open. You only have plain HTTP, and the page must show the new price.
options: Let the server send the new price to the page by itself
Let the page send a new request to ask for the price
Let a proxy start a request to the page

reasons.text: In HTTP the client starts requests, so the page must ask again.
A server can start a request whenever it has new data.
A proxy sits between the two sides, so it can start requests to the page.

tradeOff.explanation: The client starts every request, so the page must ask for the new price. The cost is delay: the page shows the old price until its next request.

decisionCards.situation: In a design review, a teammate says the server will push a message to the open page using plain HTTP. You must answer.
options: Say the page must ask, because the client starts requests
Agree, because the server starts the message when ready

reasons.text: HTTP lets both sides start a request when they want.
Only a proxy stops a server from starting a message.
The browser always starts the request. The server never does.

decisionCards.explanation: In HTTP the client starts the request, never the server. So the page must ask, which adds delay, or you need another mechanism that simulates server messages.

screens.text: A user agent is any tool that acts on behalf of the user. It sends the HTTP requests for the user. It is not the person who sits at the screen.
Most of the time the user agent is a web browser. But it can be anything. For example, a robot that crawls the web can feed a search engine index.
Example: you type a URL and press Enter. The browser sends GET / HTTP/1.1 for you. So the browser is the user agent. The person is only the user.

catch.question: What is a user agent in HTTP?
choices: The header that lists the cookies
The person who uses the website
A server program that logs visitors
Any tool that acts for the user, like a browser
catch.explanation: The user agent is any tool that acts for the user. Most often it is the web browser.

card.text: The user agent is any tool that acts for the user. Most often, it is the web browser. It can also be a program that developers use to debug their apps. The browser is always the side that starts the request.
card.example: You type a URL and press Enter. Your browser is the user agent. You test your API with a debugging program. Now that program is the user agent.

review.question: Besides a web browser, what else can be a user agent?
review.answer: A program that developers use to debug their applications.

screens.text: The server serves the document that the client asks for. To the client, it appears as one single machine.
In fact, it may be a collection of servers that share the load. This is called load balancing. So one address can hide many machines.
Imagine one request to shop.example.com. A proxy can do load balancing. It passes the request to one of three servers. The browser still sees one server.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Browser --> Balancer
  Balancer --> ServerA
  Balancer --> ServerB
  Balancer --> ServerC

catch.question: Your shop has one address, shop.example.com. How many machines can answer requests to it?
choices: Exactly one machine for each domain
One, or the address stops working
Many machines that share the load
Two: one for HTML and one for images
catch.explanation: A server looks like one machine to the client. It can be many servers that share the load.

card.text: The server serves the document that the client asks for. To the client, it looks like a single machine. In fact, it can be many servers that share the load. This is called load balancing. Other software can also help build the answer. Examples are caches, a database server, or e-commerce servers.
card.example: Your browser sends one request to shop.example.com. Behind that address, three servers share the traffic. One of them answers. To your browser, it looks like one server.

review.question: What is load balancing?
review.answer: Many servers share the requests. To the client, they look like one server.

screens.text: HTTP has two types of messages. The client sends a request to trigger an action on the server. The server sends a response, which is the answer.
Both types have the same structure. First comes a start-line. Then come optional headers. Then comes an empty line. Last comes an optional body.
Example: a sign-up form sends a request that starts with POST /users HTTP/1.1. The server answers with a response that starts with HTTP/1.1 201 Created.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Server: Request POST /users HTTP/1.1
  Server-->>Client: Response HTTP/1.1 201 Created

catch.question: What are the two types of HTTP messages?
catch.explanation: The client sends a request to start an action. The server sends a response as the answer.

card.text: HTTP has two types of messages. The client sends a request to start an action on the server. The server sends a response as the answer. Both have the same parts. First comes a start-line. Then come optional headers with metadata. An empty line ends the metadata. Last comes an optional body with the data.
card.example: Your sign-up form sends a request that starts with POST /users HTTP/1.1. The server answers with a response that starts with HTTP/1.1 201 Created.

review.question: What are the four parts of an HTTP message, in order?
review.answer: A start-line, optional headers, an empty line, and an optional body.

workedExample.problem: Your API returns JSON, but the client cannot read the body. In the raw response, the JSON starts right after the last header, on the next line.
steps: Find the start-line: HTTP/1.1 200 OK.
Find the headers: each one is a name, a colon, and a value on one line.
Look for the empty line after the headers. It is missing, so the client cannot find where the body starts.
workedExample.answer: Send one empty line after the last header. Then the client knows where the body starts.

tradeOff.situation: Your API returns JSON, but a client cannot find where the body starts. In the raw response, the JSON comes right after the last header.
options: Put the JSON in the reason phrase of the status line
Add a header called End: after the last header
Add one empty line after the last header

reasons.text: The start-line already tells the client where the body starts.
An empty line shows that the metadata is complete, so the body comes after it.
Any extra header with a colon can mark the end of the headers.

tradeOff.explanation: The empty line shows that the headers are complete, so the client finds the body. The cost is small, but if you forget this line, clients cannot read the body.

decisionCards.situation: Your endpoint answers a delete request with 204 No Content. A teammate wants to add a JSON body anyway.
options: Add the JSON body, so the client always gets data
Send no body, because a 204 response does not have one

reasons.text: Responses with a status code like 204 No Content do not have a body.
Every response must have a body, or the client sees an error.
A body is how the client learns that the request worked.

decisionCards.explanation: A 204 No Content response does not have a body, and the status code already tells the client the result. The cost is that the client gets no extra data in this answer.

screens.text: The first line of an HTTP/1.x request is called the request-line. It has three parts, always in the same order.

The parts are the method, the request target, and the protocol. The method describes the meaning of the request. The request target is usually an absolute or relative URL. The protocol is the HTTP version.
Example: in POST /users HTTP/1.1, the method is POST. The request target is /users. The protocol is HTTP/1.1.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Method --> RequestTarget
  RequestTarget --> Protocol

catch.question: What are the three parts of the first line of an HTTP/1.1 request?
choices: Method, request target, and protocol version
catch.explanation: The request-line is the method, the request target, and the protocol. For example: POST /users HTTP/1.1.

card.text: The first line of an HTTP/1.x request is the request-line. It has three parts. The method says what the client wants, for example GET or POST. The request target is usually a URL, absolute or relative. The protocol is the HTTP version. It is almost always HTTP/1.1. The versions HTTP/0.9 and HTTP/1.0 are no longer used.
card.example: In POST /users HTTP/1.1, the method is POST. The request target is /users. The protocol is HTTP/1.1.

review.question: In GET /products/42 HTTP/1.1, what is /products/42 called?
review.answer: The request target. It is usually a URL.

screens.text: The first line of a response is called the status line. It has three parts: the protocol, the status code, and the reason phrase.
The status code is a number. It says whether the request succeeded or failed. Common status codes are 200, 404, and 302.
The reason phrase is optional. It is short text that helps a human understand the result. Example: in HTTP/1.1 201 Created, the optional text is the last word.

catch.question: Which part of the status line HTTP/1.1 201 Created is optional?
choices: None of it, every part is required
catch.explanation: Created is the reason phrase. It is optional text that helps a human read the result.

card.text: The first line of a response is the status line. It has three parts. First comes the protocol, which is the HTTP version. Next comes the status code. This number says if the request succeeded or failed. Last comes the reason phrase. It is optional, short text that helps a human understand the result.
card.example: HTTP/1.1 201 Created has the protocol HTTP/1.1, the status code 201, and the reason phrase Created.

review.question: What does the status code in a status line tell you?
review.answer: Whether the request succeeded or failed.

screens.text: After the start-line come the headers. In HTTP/1.x, a header is a case-insensitive name, a colon, and a value. The whole header is on one single line.
After the last header comes one empty line. It shows that the metadata is complete. The optional body comes after it.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  StartLine --> Headers
  Headers --> EmptyLine
  EmptyLine --> Body

screens.text: Example: the last header is Content-Length: 49. Then comes an empty line. Then comes the body name=FirstName+LastName&email=bsmth%40example.com. Only PATCH, POST, and PUT requests have a body.

catch.question: How does an HTTP/1.1 message show that the headers are finished?
catch.explanation: An empty line shows that the metadata is complete. The optional body comes after it.

card.text: After the start-line come the headers. In HTTP/1.x, a header is a case-insensitive name, a colon, and a value. The whole header is on one line. Then an empty line shows that the headers are complete. The optional body comes after it. Usually, only PATCH, POST, and PUT requests have a body. Some responses, like 204 No Content, have no body.
card.example: A form request has the header Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded. Then comes one empty line. Then the body is name=FirstName+LastName&email=bsmth%40example.com.

review.question: Which three request methods usually have a body?
review.answer: PATCH, POST, and PUT.

screens.text: Every HTTP request has a method. The method shows the purpose of the request. It also shows what is expected if the request is successful.
GET requests a resource and should only retrieve data. POST submits data, often causing a change of state on the server. PUT replaces a resource. PATCH changes part of it. DELETE deletes it.
Example: GET /products/42 retrieves product 42. DELETE /products/42 deletes it. The URL is the same. The method gives the meaning.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Server: GET /products/42
  Client->>Server: DELETE /products/42

catch.question: What does the method in a request tell the server?
choices: The format of the request body
How long to keep the connection open
catch.explanation: The method shows the purpose of the request. It also shows what is expected if the request succeeds.

card.text: Each request has a method. It shows the purpose of the request and what is expected if it succeeds. GET asks for a resource and should only get data. POST sends data, often with a change of state on the server. PUT replaces the resource. PATCH changes part of it. DELETE deletes it.
card.example: GET /products/42 reads product 42. DELETE /products/42 deletes it. The URL is the same, but the method changes the meaning.

review.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
review.answer: PUT replaces the whole resource. PATCH changes only part of it.

workedExample.problem: Your teammate adds the endpoint GET /orders/9/cancel. When anyone opens this URL, order 9 is cancelled.
steps: GET should only get data.
Cancelling an order changes state on the server.
So GET is the wrong method here.
workedExample.answer: Change it to POST /orders/9/cancel. Keep GET only for reading data.

tradeOff.situation: A teammate adds GET /orders/9/cancel. Anyone who opens this URL cancels order 9, and you must pick a fix.
options: Change it to POST /orders/9/cancel
Keep GET and add a note in the API docs
Change it to HEAD, because HEAD is lighter

reasons.text: The word cancel in the URL makes GET clear enough.
Any method works, if the server code handles it.
Cancelling changes server state, and GET should only retrieve data.

tradeOff.explanation: Cancelling changes state on the server, so it needs a method that is not meant for reading. POST fits, but POST is not idempotent, so a repeated request may have extra effects.

decisionCards.situation: You design an endpoint that replaces a whole product record. The client may retry when the network drops.
options: Use PUT, which replaces the resource
Use POST, which submits data to the resource

reasons.text: PUT is not safe, so a retry of PUT is always dangerous.
PUT is idempotent: several identical calls have the same effect as one.
POST is idempotent too, so both methods are the same here.

decisionCards.explanation: PUT replaces the resource, and it is idempotent, so a retry does no harm. POST is not guaranteed to be idempotent, so a retry may add extra effects.

screens.text: A method is safe if it does not alter the state of the server. In other words, it leads to a read-only operation.
GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are safe. POST, PUT, and DELETE are not safe. Safe is about meaning. Servers can still log requests or keep statistics.
Example: GET /pageX.html HTTP/1.1 is safe. POST /pageX.html HTTP/1.1 may change the state of the server. So it is not safe.

catch.question: Which of these HTTP methods is safe?
catch.explanation: A safe method does not change the state of the server. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are safe.

card.text: A method is safe if it does not change the state of the server. In other words, it is read-only. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are safe. POST, PUT, and DELETE are not safe. Safe means read-only in meaning. The server can still write a log or keep statistics.
card.example: GET /pageX.html HTTP/1.1 is safe. POST /pageX.html HTTP/1.1 is not safe, because it may change the state of the server.

review.question: Name three safe HTTP methods.
review.answer: GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS.

screens.text: A method is idempotent if one request has the same intended effect on the server as several identical requests.
The response can differ between calls. The first DELETE /idX/delete HTTP/1.1 will likely return 200. Later calls will likely return 404. The effect on the server is the same.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Server: DELETE /idX/delete
  Server-->>Client: 200 first call
  Client->>Server: DELETE /idX/delete
  Server-->>Client: 404 later call

screens.text: All safe methods are idempotent, and so are PUT and DELETE. POST and PATCH are not guaranteed to be idempotent. A client can safely retry an idempotent request when it is unsure the request arrived.

catch.question: You send DELETE /idX/delete three times. The first call returns 200, the next two return 404. Is DELETE idempotent?
choices: No, because the status codes are different
No, because only safe methods are idempotent
Only if the server sends the same body
Yes, because the effect on the server is the same
catch.explanation: Idempotent is about the effect on the server, not the response. After the first call, the item is deleted either way.

card.text: A method is idempotent if one request has the same intended effect on the server as several identical requests. All safe methods are idempotent. PUT and DELETE are idempotent too. POST and PATCH are not guaranteed to be idempotent. A client can safely retry an idempotent request when it is not sure the request arrived. The response can still differ between calls.
card.example: The first DELETE /idX/delete HTTP/1.1 returns 200. The second returns 404, because the item is already deleted. The server state is the same after each call.

review.question: Why can a client safely retry an idempotent request?
review.answer: Several identical requests have the same intended effect as one. So a repeat does no harm.

screens.text: POST sends data to the server. The Content-Type header says the type of the request body. HTML forms usually send data with POST, and this usually changes something on the server.
POST is not safe and not idempotent. PUT is idempotent: one call is the same as many calls. Successive identical POST requests may have extra effects, such as creating the same order several times.

Example: a form sends POST /test HTTP/1.1 with Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded. The body is field1=value1&field2=value2. Because POST is not idempotent, a repeat of this request can have extra effects.

catch.question: A customer clicks Pay, and the network drops. Your client sends the same POST /orders again. What can happen?
choices: The server ignores the copy, because POST is idempotent
The server may create the same order twice
The browser always blocks the second request
The server merges both requests into one order
catch.explanation: POST is not idempotent. Identical POST requests may have extra effects, such as creating the same order several times.

card.text: POST sends data to the server. The Content-Type header says the type of the request body. POST is not safe and not idempotent. PUT is different: calling it several times has the same effect as calling it once. Identical POST requests may have extra effects, such as creating the same order several times.
card.example: A form sends POST /test HTTP/1.1 with Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded. The body is field1=value1&field2=value2. If the same request arrives twice, the server may handle it twice.

review.question: Which method is idempotent: PUT or POST?
review.answer: PUT. Identical POST requests may have extra effects.

screens.text: Every HTTP response has a status code. It is a 3-digit number. It shows if the request completed successfully. Example: a wrong URL like GET /prodcts gets 404 Not Found.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Server: GET /prodcts
  Server-->>Browser: 404 Not Found

screens.text: The first digit gives the class. 100 to 199 are informational. 200 to 299 are success. 300 to 399 are redirects. 400 to 499 are client errors. 500 to 599 are server errors.
So you can read a code you do not know. Take 429. It starts with 4, so it is in the client error class. MDN describes 429 as too many requests in a given time.

catch.question: A response has the status code 429. Without looking it up, what do you know?
choices: The request succeeded with a warning
catch.explanation: Codes from 400 to 499 are client error responses. The first digit tells you the class.

card.text: A status code is a 3-digit number in the response. It shows if the request completed successfully. Codes are grouped in five classes. 100 to 199 are informational. 200 to 299 mean success. 300 to 399 are redirects. 400 to 499 are client errors. 500 to 599 are server errors.
card.example: HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found is in the 400 class, so it is a client error. HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable is in the 500 class, so it is a server error.

review.question: Which range of status codes means a server error?

workedExample.problem: Your error dashboard counts every response that is not 200 as a failure. After a site move, it shows many failures.
steps: Read the first digit of each status code.
Most of the codes are 301. The 300 class is a redirect, not a failure.
Only the 400 and 500 classes are errors. The 400 class is the client, the 500 class is the server.
workedExample.answer: Count only 4xx and 5xx codes as errors. A 3xx code is a redirect, not a failure.

tradeOff.situation: Your API answers 200 OK and puts an error message in the body when a request fails. A partner's dashboard counts only 4xx and 5xx responses as errors.
options: Keep 200 and add an error field to the body
Use a 4xx code for client mistakes and a 5xx code for server faults
Return 500 for every failure, so there is only one rule

reasons.text: Clients always read the body, so the status code does not matter.
A 500 is the safest code because it fits every failure.
The class of the code shows who is at fault, so tools can count errors from the code alone.

tradeOff.explanation: The status code class tells every client and tool what kind of failure happened, without reading the body. The cost is that you must pick the right code each time. 500 is only the generic code when no better 5xx fits.

decisionCards.situation: Your shop is down for maintenance for 30 minutes. You must choose one status code for every page.
options: 503 Service Unavailable with a Retry-After header
500 Internal Server Error

reasons.text: 503 is for temporary conditions, and Retry-After can give the expected recovery time.
500 is more honest, because the server did not work at all.
500 is the standard code for any planned downtime.

decisionCards.explanation: 503 says the server is not ready, often because of maintenance, and Retry-After can show when to come back. The cost is that you must remember to add the header.

screens.text: A 2xx code means the request succeeded. But what success means depends on the HTTP method. For a GET, 200 OK means the resource was fetched and sent in the message body.

When a request creates something, a more exact code exists. 201 Created means the request succeeded and a new resource was created. A server typically sends it after a POST request, or after some PUT requests.
Example: a sign-up form sends POST /users. The server creates the user and answers 201 Created. Later, GET /users/123 returns 200 OK with the user data.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Server: POST /users
  Server-->>Browser: 201 Created

catch.question: Your API creates a new user from a POST request. Which status code fits best?
catch.explanation: 201 Created means the request succeeded and created a new resource. It is typical after a POST.

card.text: Codes from 200 to 299 mean the request succeeded. 200 OK means the request succeeded. What success means depends on the HTTP method. 201 Created means the request succeeded and created a new resource. A server typically sends it after a POST request, or after some PUT requests.
card.example: A sign-up form sends POST /users. The server answers HTTP/1.1 201 Created. Later, GET /users/123 gets HTTP/1.1 200 OK with the user data.

review.question: When does a server typically send 201 Created?
review.answer: After a POST, or some PUT requests, that create a new resource.

screens.text: A redirect response has a status code that starts with 3. It tells the browser that the page it asked for is available at another URL.
The new URL is in a Location header on the same response. When a browser gets a redirect, it loads the URL from that header at once. Users rarely notice it.

Example: an old page moved. The server answers 301 Moved Permanently with Location: https://example.com/new-page. The browser then opens the new page. 301 and 308 are permanent. 302, 303, and 307 are temporary.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Server: GET /old-page
  Server-->>Browser: 301 and Location header
  Browser->>Server: GET /new-page

catch.question: How does the browser know where to go after a 301 response?
choices: It reads a link in the response body
It asks the DNS server again
catch.explanation: A redirect response has a Location header with the new URL. The browser loads that URL at once.

card.text: Redirect responses have status codes that start with 3. They also have a Location header with the URL to go to. The browser loads that new URL at once. 301 and 308 are permanent, so search engines update the old URL. 302, 303, and 307 are temporary. A server uses 303 See Other after a POST. Then a page refresh does not repeat the action.
card.example: Your shop moved a page. The old URL answers HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently with Location: https://example.com/new-page. The browser opens the new page.

review.question: Which two redirect codes are permanent?
review.answer: 301 and 308. Search engines then update the old URL.

screens.text: Codes from 400 to 499 are client errors. Three of them are easy to mix up: 401, 403, and 404. Start with 404 Not Found. It means the server cannot find the resource.
401 Unauthorized really means unauthenticated. The client must prove who it is. Example: a visitor who is not logged in asks for GET /account and gets 401.

403 Forbidden means the client has no access rights. Unlike 401, the server already knows who the client is, but it refuses to give the resource. Example: a normal customer asks for GET /admin and gets 403.

catch.question: A logged-in customer opens another customer's invoice. The server knows who they are, but blocks them. Which code fits?
catch.explanation: 403 means the server knows the client, but the client has no access rights. 401 means the client must authenticate first.

card.text: Codes from 400 to 499 are client errors. Three of them are easy to mix up. 401 Unauthorized really means unauthenticated: the client must prove who it is. 403 Forbidden means the server knows the client, but the client has no access rights. 404 Not Found means the server cannot find the resource. A server may send 404 instead of 403 to hide that a resource exists.
card.example: Not logged in: GET /account returns 401. Logged in as a normal customer: GET /admin returns 403. A wrong URL: GET /prodcts returns 404.

review.question: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
review.answer: With 401, the client must authenticate first. With 403, the server knows the client, but it has no access.

screens.text: Codes from 500 to 599 are server errors. 500 Internal Server Error is generic. The server sends it when it cannot find a more appropriate 5xx code.
502 Bad Gateway is more exact. It means a server that works as a gateway got an invalid response while it handled your request.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Gateway: GET /shop
  Gateway->>App: GET /shop
  App-->>Gateway: invalid response
  Gateway-->>Browser: 502 Bad Gateway

screens.text: 503 Service Unavailable means the server is not ready. Common causes are maintenance or overload. Use it for temporary conditions. The server can add a Retry-After header with the expected recovery time.

catch.question: Your shop sits behind a gateway. The gateway gets an invalid response from your app server. Which code fits?
catch.explanation: 502 means a server that works as a gateway got an invalid response. 500 is the generic code when nothing better fits.

card.text: Codes from 500 to 599 are server errors. 500 Internal Server Error is generic. The server sends it when no better 5xx code fits. 502 Bad Gateway means a server that works as a gateway got an invalid response. 503 Service Unavailable means the server is not ready. Common causes are maintenance or too much traffic. Use 503 for temporary conditions.
card.example: During maintenance, your shop answers HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable. It also sends a friendly page about the problem. It can add a Retry-After header with the expected recovery time.

review.question: Which server error code fits a temporary condition, like maintenance?
review.answer: 503 Service Unavailable.

screens.text: The Content-Type header gives the media type of a resource. In a response, it tells the client the type of the returned data. Example: Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8.
Requests use it too. In a POST or a PUT, the client uses Content-Type to name the type of content it sends. A file upload can send multipart/form-data.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Server: POST with Content-Type multipart/form-data
  Server-->>Client: Response with Content-Type text/html

screens.text: A strict server may answer with a 415 client error if it dislikes the type. Browsers may ignore the value if they do MIME sniffing. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops that.

catch.question: In a POST request, what does the Content-Type header describe?
choices: The type of content the client wants back
The type of content the client is sending
catch.explanation: In requests like POST or PUT, Content-Type says what type of content is sent.

card.text: The Content-Type header gives the media type of the resource. In a response, it tells the client the type of the returned data. In a POST or PUT request, it tells the server the type of content sent. A strict server may answer with a 415 client error. Browsers may ignore the value if they do MIME sniffing. The header X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops that.
card.example: A page response sends Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8. A file upload form sends Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=ExampleBoundaryString.

review.question: What does Content-Type tell the client in a response?
review.answer: The media type of the returned data, for example text/html.

workedExample.problem: Your API returns JSON. A customer app cannot parse it. The response header says Content-Type: text/html.
steps: The body is JSON, but the header says HTML.
The client reads Content-Type to learn the media type of the data.
The MIME type for JSON is application/json.
workedExample.answer: Send Content-Type: application/json with the JSON body.

tradeOff.situation: Your site serves files that users upload. A security review asks that browsers must not guess the type of those files.
options: Send the right Content-Type and add X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Rely on the file extension, because browsers check it
Send no Content-Type, because browsers always guess the right type

reasons.text: Browsers use the file extension, so the header does not matter.
The nosniff value stops MIME sniffing, so browsers follow the type that you declare.
Sniffing always finds the correct type, so a header is extra work.

tradeOff.explanation: A correct Content-Type plus nosniff makes browsers follow the type you declare. The cost is that you must send the right type for every file.

decisionCards.situation: A client sends a JSON body to your API, but its Content-Type says text/plain. You can accept it or refuse it.
options: Accept it and guess that the body is JSON
Answer 415 and ask for the right type

reasons.text: Guessing is friendlier, because the body always shows its true type.
A 415 is a server error, so it hurts your uptime.
A strict server may answer with a 415 client error when the type is wrong.

decisionCards.explanation: A strict server may return 415, so the client learns the header is wrong. The cost is that some careless clients will fail until they fix the header.

screens.text: A MIME type, or media type, says the nature and format of a file. It has a type and a subtype, with a slash between and no spaces. Example: text/html.
Browsers use the MIME type, not the file extension, to decide how to process a URL. The server sends the MIME type in the Content-Type header, so the header must be correct.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Server: GET styles.css
  Server-->>Browser: Content-Type text/plain

screens.text: CSS files must be sent as text/css. A browser can load a CSS file from a link element. If it is text/plain, the browser does not treat it as CSS. So styles.css sent as text/plain does not style the page.

catch.question: Your server sends styles.css with Content-Type: text/plain. What do most browsers do?
choices: They do not treat it as CSS, so they ignore it
They see the .css extension and apply the styles
They show the CSS code as text on the page
They ask the user where to save the file
catch.explanation: Browsers use the MIME type, not the file extension. Most browsers do not treat CSS sent as text/plain as CSS, so they ignore it.

card.text: A MIME type, or media type, says the nature and format of a file. It has a type and a subtype, with a slash between and no spaces. An optional parameter can follow, like charset=UTF-8. MIME types are case-insensitive, but people usually write them in lowercase. Browsers use the MIME type, not the file extension, to decide how to handle a URL.
card.example: text/html is for HTML pages. application/json is for JSON data. text/plain;charset=UTF-8 is a UTF-8 text file. CSS must be sent as text/css, or most browsers ignore it.

review.question: What does a browser use to decide how to handle a file?
review.answer: The MIME type in the Content-Type header, not the file extension.

screens.text: Content negotiation is how a client and a server agree on a content type. The client makes proposals. The server uses content negotiation to select one of them.
The proposals go in the Accept request header. It lists the MIME types that the client can understand. A weight written ;q= shows the order of preference. image/* means any image type.

The server tells the client its choice in the Content-Type response header. Example: a browser sends Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8. The server can answer with Content-Type: text/html.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Server: Accept lists text/html first
  Server-->>Browser: Content-Type text/html

catch.question: Which request header tells the server which media types the client can understand?
catch.explanation: The client lists the media types it understands in Accept. The server picks one and names it in Content-Type.

card.text: The Accept request header lists the MIME types that the client can understand. The server uses content negotiation to pick one. Then it names its choice in the Content-Type response header. Each type can have a weight, ;q=, that shows the order of preference. image/* means any image type. */* means any media type.
card.example: A browser opens a page and sends Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8. The server picks HTML. It answers with Content-Type: text/html.

review.question: After content negotiation, which header tells the client what the server chose?
review.answer: The Content-Type response header.

screens.text: Think of a shopping basket. You add a shoe with one request. Then you open the basket page with a second request. Does the server link these two requests?
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Server: Request 1 add a shoe
  Server-->>Browser: Answer 1
  Browser->>Server: Request 2 open the basket
  Server-->>Browser: Answer 2

screens.text: HTTP is stateless. There is no link between two requests that follow each other. This is true even on the same connection. Each request stands alone.
This is a problem for pages like shopping baskets. But HTTP is not sessionless. Cookies are added to the workflow. They let requests share the same context. A cookie is what links your two requests.

catch.question: Your browser sends two requests on the same connection. What does HTTP itself link between them?
choices: It links them because they share one connection
Nothing, because each request stands alone
It links them by the client IP address
It links them when both use the GET method
catch.explanation: HTTP is stateless. There is no link between two requests, even on the same connection.

card.text: HTTP is stateless. There is no link between two requests, even when they use the same connection. This is a problem for some pages, for example a shopping basket. But HTTP is not sessionless. HTTP cookies add a session on top of HTTP. Then many requests can share the same state.
card.example: You add a shoe to your basket with one request. Then you open the basket page with a second request. HTTP itself has no link between these two requests. A cookie is what links them.

review.question: What does it mean that HTTP is stateless?
review.answer: There is no link between two requests. Each request stands alone, even on the same connection.

workedExample.problem: A customer adds items to the basket. On the next page, the basket is empty again.
steps: Each page load is a new HTTP request.
HTTP does not link two requests by itself.
The server needs something in each request that says which basket it is.
workedExample.answer: Set a cookie with a session id. The browser sends it back with each request.

tradeOff.situation: A customer adds items to the basket, but the next page shows an empty basket. A teammate wants to fix it at the connection level.
options: Keep one open connection for each customer
Switch to HTTP/2, because it sends messages over one connection
Use a cookie that links each request to the basket state on the server

reasons.text: Cookies add a session through headers, so each request shares the same state.
A shared connection links requests, so a longer connection is enough.
HTTP/2 makes HTTP stateful, so an upgrade removes the need for sessions.

tradeOff.explanation: Cookies use header extensibility, so each request carries the context that links it to the basket on the server. The cost is that the server must keep and look up that state.

decisionCards.situation: Your server must know which user sent each request. A teammate says the open connection is enough.
options: Send a session cookie with every request
Trust the open connection to identify the user

reasons.text: A shared connection links requests, so the server already knows the user.
A cookie travels in headers with each request, so requests share the same state.
HTTP keeps state, but only over HTTPS.

decisionCards.explanation: HTTP has no link between requests, even on one connection, so a cookie must add the link. The cost is that the server must store the state for each session.

screens.text: A browser can send many requests over one connection. Many people think the connection links them. The next screen shows if that is true.
HTTP is stateless. There is no link between two requests that follow each other on the same connection. HTTP does not link a request to the request before it.
Example: a request for GET /cart does not say who you are. HTTP alone cannot tell that two requests belong together. This makes pages like shopping baskets hard to build.

catch.question: Which statement about HTTP is true?
choices: The TCP connection remembers the user between requests
HTTP/2 makes HTTP stateful because it uses one connection
HTTP keeps state, but only over HTTPS
HTTP has no link between two requests
catch.explanation: HTTP is stateless. Sharing one connection does not link two requests.

card.text: In HTTP, each request stands alone. HTTP does not link a request to the request before it. This is true even when both requests share one connection. So HTTP alone cannot tell that two requests belong together. This makes some pages hard to build, for example a shopping basket.
card.example: Your browser sends GET /cart HTTP/1.1 with Host: shop.example.com. This request does not say who you are. HTTP has no link to your earlier request that added an item.

review.question: Does sharing one TCP connection link two HTTP requests?
review.answer: No. HTTP has no link between two requests, even on the same connection.

screens.text: The core of HTTP is stateless. But HTTP is not sessionless. A site can still keep a session, for example for a shopping basket.
HTTP can get new headers. This is header extensibility. HTTP cookies use it. They are added to the workflow, so each request shares the same context, or the same state.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Server: Request with a Cookie header
  Server-->>Browser: Basket for that session

screens.text: So cookies link requests with the state of the server. This creates sessions, even though basic HTTP is stateless. That is why a basket can stay full from page to page.

catch.question: HTTP is stateless. How do sites still keep you logged in across pages?
choices: HTTP cookies add a session through headers
The browser keeps one TCP connection per user
The server remembers the user's IP address
HTTP/1.1 has a built-in login method
catch.explanation: Cookies travel in HTTP headers. Each request carries the cookie, so the requests share the same state.

card.text: The core of HTTP is stateless, but HTTP is not sessionless. You can add new headers to HTTP. Cookies use this to create a session. Each request carries the cookie, so the requests share the same context. This links your requests with the state on the server.
card.example: Your browser sends Cookie: sessionId=38afes7a8 with each request. The server reads the id and finds your basket.

review.question: What adds a session on top of stateless HTTP?
review.answer: HTTP cookies. They travel in headers, so requests can share the same state.

screens.text: A cookie is a small piece of data. A server sends it to your web browser. Cookies are mainly used for three things: session management, personalization and tracking.
The browser may store the cookie. Later, the browser sends the cookie back to the same server with new requests. So the browser holds the cookie between requests.
Example: the server answers with Set-Cookie: yummy_cookie=chocolate. The browser stores it. Your next request to that server has Cookie: yummy_cookie=chocolate.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Server: GET /sample_page.html
  Server-->>Browser: Set-Cookie yummy_cookie=chocolate
  Browser->>Server: Cookie yummy_cookie=chocolate

catch.question: Who stores a cookie and sends it back to the server?
choices: The proxy between you and the server
catch.explanation: The server sends the cookie. The browser may store it and send it back with later requests.

card.text: A cookie is a small piece of data. A server sends it to your browser. The browser may store it. Then the browser sends it back to the same server with later requests. Cookies are mainly used for session management, personalization and tracking. Session management means things like sign-in status and shopping cart contents.
card.example: The response has Set-Cookie: yummy_cookie=chocolate. Your next request to that server has Cookie: yummy_cookie=chocolate.

review.question: Name the three main uses of cookies.
review.answer: Session management, personalization and tracking.

workedExample.problem: Customers must log in again every time they restart the browser.
steps: Look at the Set-Cookie header of the login cookie.
It has no Expires and no Max-Age, so it is a session cookie.
The browser deletes session cookies when the current session ends.
workedExample.answer: Add Max-Age. For example, Max-Age=2592000 keeps the cookie for 30 days.

tradeOff.situation: Your shop keeps the sign-in status in a cookie. A third-party script runs on your pages, and you do not want it to read that cookie. Your own pages never need to read it.
options: Add the Secure attribute to the cookie
Add the HttpOnly attribute to the cookie
Add a short Max-Age to the cookie

reasons.text: HttpOnly forbids JavaScript from reading the cookie, and the browser still sends it to the server.
Secure stops JavaScript from reading the cookie when the page uses HTTPS.
A short Max-Age makes the cookie unreadable for scripts while it lives.

tradeOff.explanation: HttpOnly keeps the cookie out of reach of JavaScript, for example through Document.cookie. The cost is that your own front-end code cannot read the cookie either.

decisionCards.situation: Your widget runs on other sites. Its cookie must be sent with cross-site requests. You must choose a SameSite value.
options: SameSite=Lax
SameSite=None, together with Secure

reasons.text: Lax sends the cookie with every cross-site request.
SameSite=None works without the Secure attribute.
None sends the cookie with cross-site requests, and it needs Secure.

decisionCards.explanation: None sends the cookie with both same-site and cross-site requests, and Secure must also be set. The cost is that the cookie has less SameSite protection against cross-site attacks.

screens.text: A server gives a cookie to the browser in the response. It uses the Set-Cookie response header. Each Set-Cookie header sets one separate cookie.
One response can have one or more Set-Cookie headers. Example: Set-Cookie: yummy_cookie=chocolate and Set-Cookie: tasty_cookie=strawberry. The browser stores both cookies.
When a new request is made, the browser usually sends the stored cookies for the current domain. It uses the Cookie request header. Example: Cookie: yummy_cookie=chocolate; tasty_cookie=strawberry.

catch.question: Which header does a server use to give your browser a cookie?
catch.explanation: The server sends Set-Cookie in the response. The browser sends Cookie in later requests.

card.text: The server sends a cookie in the Set-Cookie response header. One response can have one or more Set-Cookie headers. Each one sets a separate cookie. On later requests, the browser sends the cookies back in the Cookie request header. A semicolon splits the cookies in that header.
card.example: The response has two headers: Set-Cookie: yummy_cookie=chocolate and Set-Cookie: tasty_cookie=strawberry. Your next request has one header: Cookie: yummy_cookie=chocolate; tasty_cookie=strawberry.

review.question: Which header carries cookies from the browser to the server?
review.answer: The Cookie request header, for example Cookie: yummy_cookie=chocolate.

screens.text: A cookie without Expires and without Max-Age is a session cookie. The browser removes it when the session ends. A session ends when the client shuts down.
Many browsers have a session restore feature. It saves all tabs and restores them next time. Session cookies are restored too, as if the browser was never closed.
A permanent cookie is removed at a date or after a time. Expires sets the date. Max-Age sets the seconds. Example: Max-Age=2592000. If both are set, Max-Age has precedence.

catch.question: A cookie has no Expires and no Max-Age. When is it deleted?
catch.explanation: This is a session cookie. The browser removes it when the session ends.

card.text: A session cookie has no Expires and no Max-Age attribute. The browser removes it when the session ends, which is when the browser shuts down. Many browsers can restore a session, and then session cookies come back too. A permanent cookie ends at the Expires date, or after Max-Age seconds. Max-Age wins when both are set.
card.example: Set-Cookie: id=a3fWa; Max-Age=2592000 keeps the cookie for 2592000 seconds. Set-Cookie: id=a3fWa; Expires=Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT keeps it until that date.

review.question: Expires and Max-Age are both set. Which one wins?
review.answer: Max-Age. It has precedence over Expires.

screens.text: The Secure attribute limits how a cookie is sent. The browser sends the cookie only with an encrypted HTTPS request. It never sends it with plain HTTP. Localhost is an exception, but Safari does not support that.
The HttpOnly attribute limits who can read a cookie. JavaScript cannot access the cookie, for example through Document.cookie.

Example: Set-Cookie: id=a3fWa; Expires=Thu, 21 Oct 2021 07:28:00 GMT; Secure; HttpOnly. This cookie goes only over HTTPS, and scripts cannot read it. HttpOnly helps against cross-site scripting attacks.

catch.question: What does the HttpOnly attribute do?
choices: It stops JavaScript from reading the cookie
It sends the cookie only over HTTP, not HTTPS
It sends the cookie only to the same site
It deletes the cookie when the tab closes
catch.explanation: HttpOnly blocks access from JavaScript, for example from Document.cookie. Only the server can use the cookie.

card.text: A cookie with Secure is only sent with encrypted HTTPS requests. It is never sent with plain HTTP. The one exception is localhost, but Safari does not support it. A cookie with HttpOnly cannot be read by JavaScript, for example with Document.cookie. Only the server can use it.
card.example: Set-Cookie: id=a3fWa; Expires=Thu, 21 Oct 2021 07:28:00 GMT; Secure; HttpOnly

review.question: What does the Secure attribute do?
review.answer: The cookie is only sent with HTTPS requests, never with plain HTTP. Localhost is the one exception.

screens.text: SameSite tells the browser when to send a cookie with cross-site requests. Strict sends it only for requests from the site that set it. Lax also sends it when the user navigates to that site from another site.
None sends the cookie with both same-site and cross-site requests. When you set SameSite=None, the Secure attribute must also be set. Without SameSite, some browsers treat the cookie as Lax.
Example: a widget used on other sites sets Set-Cookie: widget_session=xyz789; SameSite=None; Secure. A shop cart cookie can use SameSite=Strict instead.

catch.question: You set SameSite=None on a cookie. What must the cookie also have?
catch.explanation: SameSite=None sends the cookie with cross-site requests. The Secure attribute must also be set.

card.text: SameSite controls when the browser sends a cookie with cross-site requests. Strict sends it only with requests from the site that set it. Lax also sends it when you follow a link to that site from another site. None sends it with same-site and cross-site requests. None also needs Secure. Some browsers use Lax when there is no SameSite attribute.
card.example: The shop sets its cart cookie with Set-Cookie: cart=abc123; SameSite=Strict. A widget used on other sites sets Set-Cookie: widget_session=xyz789; SameSite=None; Secure.

review.question: Which SameSite value sends a cookie only with requests from the site that set it?
review.answer: Strict.

screens.text: Many machines relay HTTP messages between your browser and the server. Most of them work at the transport, network or physical level. HTTP does not see them.

Machines that work at the application layer are called proxies. A proxy sits between the client and the server and relays HTTP messages. Some proxies pass a request on unchanged. Others change it first.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Browser --> Proxy
  Proxy --> Server

screens.text: Proxies can do many jobs: caching, filtering, load balancing, authentication and logging. Example: an antivirus scan on each page is filtering. Storing a history of requests is logging.

catch.question: What is a proxy in HTTP?
choices: A copy of a web page that the browser keeps
A server that turns a domain name into an IP address
A second TCP connection for slow pages
A machine between client and server that relays HTTP messages
catch.explanation: A proxy works at the application layer. It sits between the browser and the server and relays HTTP messages.

card.text: Many machines relay HTTP messages between your browser and the server. Most work at lower levels, so HTTP does not see them. Machines at the application layer are called proxies. A transparent proxy forwards requests without changes. A non-transparent proxy changes the request first. Proxies can do caching, filtering, load balancing, authentication and logging.
card.example: A company proxy runs an antivirus scan on each page before your browser gets it. That is filtering. Another proxy stores a log of every request. That is logging.

review.question: What is the difference between a transparent and a non-transparent proxy?
review.answer: A transparent proxy forwards requests unchanged. A non-transparent proxy changes the request before it passes it on.

workedExample.problem: Staff in one office load the same shop logo many times a day.
steps: A proxy sits between their browsers and the server.
A caching proxy keeps a copy of the logo.
Later requests get the copy, so the server sends less.
workedExample.answer: Use a proxy that caches public files, such as images.

tradeOff.situation: Your site runs on three web servers. You want to spread the load and cache pictures, without changing each server.
options: Ask customers to use a different browser
Let each server cache on its own
Put a proxy in front of the servers

reasons.text: Servers spread the load between themselves without help.
A proxy between clients and servers can balance the load and cache answers.
The browser decides which server gets each request.

tradeOff.explanation: A proxy in front of the servers can balance the load and cache answers in one place. The cost is one more machine between customers and your servers.

decisionCards.situation: Your company wants to block some websites for its staff.
options: Put a filtering proxy between the staff browsers and the internet
Ask each website to block your staff

reasons.text: Websites must block any company that asks them to.
A filter only works inside each website's own server.
A proxy between browsers and servers can filter the requests.

decisionCards.explanation: A proxy sees the requests on the way, so it can filter them in one place. The cost is one more machine on every request.

screens.text: A forward proxy gives proxy services to a client or to a group of clients. It acts on behalf of clients. It is also called a gateway, or just a proxy.
Forward proxies store and forward Internet services, like DNS or web pages. This reduces and controls the bandwidth that the group uses.
A forward proxy can also hide your IP address while you browse. Example: all laptops in an office use one forward proxy. The proxy can hide each laptop IP address from web servers.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Laptops --> ForwardProxy
  ForwardProxy --> WebServers

catch.question: A forward proxy acts for whom?
choices: For the web servers behind it
For a client or a group of clients
catch.explanation: A forward proxy works on behalf of clients. A reverse proxy works for servers.

card.text: A forward proxy works on behalf of a client or a group of clients. It is also called a gateway, or just a proxy. It can store and forward services like DNS or web pages. This reduces and controls the bandwidth the group uses. A forward proxy can also hide your IP address while you browse.
card.example: All laptops in an office send web requests through one forward proxy. The proxy can hide each laptop's IP address from the web servers.

review.question: Name one reason to use a forward proxy.
review.answer: To reduce and control the bandwidth of a group, or to hide the client's IP address.

screens.text: A reverse proxy does the opposite of a forward proxy. A forward proxy acts on behalf of clients and can hide them. A reverse proxy can hide the identity of servers.
A reverse proxy is used to control and protect access to a server. One use is load balancing. It distributes the load to several web servers. It can also cache static content and compress content.
Example: customers open https://shop.example.com. A reverse proxy sends each request to one of three web servers. The customers do not see which server answered.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Customers --> ReverseProxy
  ReverseProxy --> Server1
  ReverseProxy --> Server2
  ReverseProxy --> Server3

catch.question: Your site has three web servers behind one public address. What spreads requests between them?
catch.explanation: A reverse proxy sits in front of servers. Load balancing is one of its main uses.

card.text: A reverse proxy does the opposite of a forward proxy. A forward proxy acts for clients and can hide them. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and can hide them. It controls and protects access to a server. Common uses are load balancing, authentication, decryption, caching and compression.
card.example: Customers open https://shop.example.com. A reverse proxy takes each request and sends it to one of three web servers. The customers do not see which server answered.

review.question: What can a reverse proxy hide?
review.answer: The identity of the servers behind it. A forward proxy hides clients instead.

screens.text: DNS means Domain Name System. It keeps a list of domain names and the resources linked to them, such as IP addresses.
The main job of DNS is to turn a human-friendly domain name into a numeric IP address. This is called a DNS lookup. With the IP address, your browser can talk to the web server.
Example: a DNS lookup for mozilla.org can give the IP address 192.0.2.172. A reverse DNS lookup does the opposite. It finds the domain name for an IP address.

catch.question: You type shop.example.com. What must be found before your browser can reach the server?
choices: The HTTP version of the server
catch.explanation: A DNS lookup turns the domain name into an IP address. Computers reach a server by its IP address.

card.text: DNS means Domain Name System. It keeps a list of domain names and the resources linked to them, such as IP addresses. Its main job is to turn a domain name into a numeric IP address. This is called a DNS lookup. A reverse DNS lookup does the opposite. It finds the domain name for an IP address.
card.example: A DNS lookup for example.com can give an IP address such as 192.0.2.172. A reverse DNS lookup starts from 192.0.2.172 and finds the name.

review.question: What is a DNS lookup?
review.answer: Mapping a domain name to its IP address.

workedExample.problem: A visitor types shop.example.com, but computers connect to IP addresses.
steps: The browser asks DNS for the IP address of the name.
DNS answers with the numeric IP address.
The browser then connects to that address.
workedExample.answer: DNS turns the domain name into the IP address the browser connects to.

tradeOff.situation: Your shop moves to a new server with a new IP address. Customers still type the same name.
options: Ask customers to type the new IP address
Change the DNS record to the new IP address
Give the shop a new domain name

reasons.text: DNS turns the name into the IP address, so only the record must change.
People remember IP addresses better than names.
A new server always needs a new domain name.

tradeOff.explanation: Customers keep the name, and DNS points it to the new address. The cost is that you must update the record and check it.

decisionCards.situation: Your logs show the IP address 192.0.2.172. You want to know which domain name belongs to it.
options: Do a DNS lookup on the IP address
Do a reverse DNS lookup on the IP address

reasons.text: A normal DNS lookup maps an IP address to its domain name.
A reverse DNS lookup finds the domain name that belongs to an IP address.
A reverse DNS lookup only works for names that your company controls.

decisionCards.explanation: A reverse DNS lookup is used to find the domain name for an IP address. The cost is that it answers only this reverse question and does not tell you if the web server works.

screens.text: You type a domain name in your browser. First, the browser asks your computer if it already knows the IP address. The computer checks its local DNS cache.
If the IP address is in the cache, the name becomes the IP address. The browser then talks to the web server. No more steps are needed.
If the computer does not know the IP address, it asks a DNS server. A DNS server tells your computer which IP address matches each registered domain name. Then the browser contacts the web server.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Computer: IP of mozilla.org?
  Computer->>DNSServer: Not in cache. Which IP?
  DNSServer-->>Computer: IP address

source.title: MDN: What is a domain name?

catch.question: You type example.com. Where does your computer look first for the IP address?
catch.explanation: Your computer checks its local DNS cache first. It asks a DNS server only when the address is not there.

card.text: You type a domain name in the browser. First, your computer checks its local DNS cache for the IP address. If the address is there, the browser can talk to the web server. If not, your computer asks a DNS server. The DNS server tells your computer which IP address matches the name.
card.example: You type example.com in the address bar. Your computer checks its local DNS cache. There is no match, so it asks a DNS server. With the IP address, your browser contacts the web server.

source.title: MDN: What is a domain name?

review.question: What does a DNS server tell your computer?
review.answer: Which IP address matches a registered domain name.

screens.text: A domain name has parts that are separated by dots. You read them from right to left. The rightmost part is the top-level domain, or TLD.
The label right before the TLD is the secondary level domain, or SLD. For a domain you control, you can create subdomains with different content.
Example: in developer.mozilla.org, org is the TLD. The label mozilla is the SLD. The label developer is a subdomain.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  org --> mozilla
  mozilla --> developer

source.title: MDN: What is a domain name?

catch.question: How do you read the parts of a domain name?
choices: From the longest label to the shortest
In any order, because the parts are not ranked
catch.explanation: The parts are split by dots and read from right to left. The top-level domain comes first.

card.text: A domain name has parts called labels, split by dots. You read them from right to left. The rightmost part is the top-level domain (TLD), for example com or org. The label just before the TLD is the secondary level domain (SLD). You can create subdomains in front of a domain you control. Some TLDs have rules: gov is only for government departments.
card.example: In shop.example.com, com is the TLD. The label example is the SLD. The label shop is a subdomain.

source.title: MDN: What is a domain name?

review.question: Which label is the secondary level domain (SLD)?
review.answer: The label right before the TLD, like example in shop.example.com.

screens.text: HTTP/1.1 lets you reuse one TCP connection for many requests. But clients still had to wait for each resource to download before asking for the next one. A request line looks like this: GET /logo.png HTTP/1.1.

HTTP/2 is a binary protocol, not a text protocol. It sends parallel requests over the same connection. It also compresses headers. HTTP/2 needed no changes to websites. Only an up-to-date server and a recent browser were needed.
HTTP/3 has the same semantics as earlier versions of HTTP. It changes the transport layer: it uses QUIC instead of TCP. So the big change across versions is how messages travel over the connection.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Semantics --> TCP
  Semantics --> QUIC
  QUIC --> UDP

catch.question: What changed most from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 to HTTP/3?
choices: The methods, like GET and POST
How messages travel over the connection
catch.explanation: HTTP/2 did not need changes to websites. HTTP/3 keeps the same semantics but changes the transport.

card.text: HTTP/1.1 reuses one TCP connection for many requests. But each request still waits for the one before it. HTTP/2 is binary and multiplexed. It sends parallel requests over one connection and compresses headers. HTTP/3 keeps the same semantics as earlier versions. But it uses QUIC instead of TCP. QUIC runs over UDP.
card.example: Your product page needs 30 images. With HTTP/1.1, each image waits for the one before it on a connection. With HTTP/2, the 30 requests can share one connection at the same time.

review.question: Name one change that HTTP/2 brought.
review.answer: Multiplexing: parallel requests over one connection. It also compresses headers.

workedExample.problem: Your shop page loads 40 small files over HTTP/1.1. The files arrive one after another on each connection.
steps: HTTP/1.1 reuses the connection, but each request waits for the one before.
This wait is called head-of-line blocking.
HTTP/2 sends parallel requests over the same connection.
workedExample.answer: Turn on HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 on your server or reverse proxy. Websites need no changes for HTTP/2.

tradeOff.situation: Your shop page loads 30 images and feels slow. A teammate wants to rewrite the site to fix it.
options: Rewrite the site code to work in a new way
Keep HTTP/1.1 and wait for browsers to change
Turn on HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 on the server

reasons.text: HTTP/2 only works if the site code sends its files in a new format
HTTP/2 sends parallel requests over one connection and needs no change to the website
HTTP/3 replaces the HTTP methods, so the site must be rewritten

tradeOff.explanation: HTTP/2 gives parallel requests over one connection, and the website itself does not change. The cost is that you need an up-to-date server and a recent browser.

decisionCards.situation: Many of your users load pages on weak phone networks. With HTTP/2, one lost packet can block all streams.
options: Add HTTP/3 next to HTTP/2
Stay on HTTP/2 only

reasons.text: Packet loss only hurts HTTP/1.1, so HTTP/2 is already safe
HTTP/3 stops packets from getting lost
QUIC handles packet loss for each stream alone, so only one stream waits

decisionCards.explanation: QUIC runs streams over UDP. It handles packet loss for each stream, so only the stream with data in the lost packet waits. The cost is server work, because HTTP/3 uses QUIC instead of TCP.

screens.text: In a short-lived connection, each request gets its own connection. So a TCP handshake happens before every request. The TCP handshake is time-consuming. HTTP/1.0 used this model by default.
A persistent connection stays open for a period of time. It can be reused for several requests. It is also called a keep-alive connection. Idle connections are still closed after some time.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Server: Request 1
  Server-->>Browser: Response 1
  Browser->>Server: Request 2 on the same connection
  Server-->>Browser: Response 2

screens.text: In HTTP/1.1, persistence is the default. The short-lived model is used only when the Connection header is sent with the value close. For example, a response with Connection: close ends the connection.

catch.question: In HTTP/1.1, when does a connection close right after one response?
choices: Always, because it is the default
When the Connection header is close
catch.explanation: Persistence is the default in HTTP/1.1. A short-lived connection is used only with Connection: close.

card.text: By default in HTTP/1.0, each request gets its own TCP connection. So a TCP handshake happens before each request. A persistent connection stays open and is reused for several requests. It is also called a keep-alive connection. In HTTP/1.1, persistence is the default. Idle connections still close after some time.
card.example: A response with the header Connection: close ends the connection after it. Without this header, an HTTP/1.1 connection stays open for more requests.

review.question: What does a persistent connection save you?
review.answer: A new TCP handshake for each request. One connection is reused for several requests.

screens.text: In HTTP/1.1, the connection could be reused. But a client had to wait for each resource to download before it asked for the next one.
HTTP/2 is a binary protocol. You cannot read or write it by hand. It also compresses headers, because headers are often similar between requests.
HTTP/2 is multiplexed. Parallel requests can be made over the same connection. A browser can ask for style.css, app.js and logo.png at the same time on one connection.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>Server: GET style.css
  Browser->>Server: GET app.js
  Browser->>Server: GET logo.png

catch.question: What does multiplexing in HTTP/2 mean?
choices: Many TCP connections for one page
Sending one request to many servers
Splitting a site across many domains
Parallel requests over the same connection
catch.explanation: HTTP/2 sends parallel requests over one connection.

card.text: HTTP/2 is a multiplexed protocol. Parallel requests can go over the same connection. In HTTP/1.1, a client had to wait for each resource before it asked for the next one. This wait is called head-of-line blocking. HTTP/2 is also binary, not text. You cannot read or write it by hand.
card.example: Your browser needs style.css, app.js and logo.png from shop.example.com. With HTTP/2, it sends all three requests at once on one connection.

review.question: What is head-of-line blocking in HTTP/1.1?
review.answer: The client waits for one resource to download before it asks for the next one.

screens.text: HTTP/3 has the same semantics as earlier versions of HTTP. The change is in the transport layer. HTTP/2 runs over one single TCP connection.
With TCP, packet loss detection and retransmission can block all streams. So one lost packet can stop every request that shares the connection.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC instead of TCP. QUIC runs multiple streams over UDP. It handles packet loss for each stream alone. So only the stream with data in the lost packet is blocked.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  HTTP3 --> QUIC
  QUIC --> UDP

catch.question: What is the main change in HTTP/3?
choices: New HTTP methods and status codes
It uses QUIC instead of TCP
