It sends all data as plain text
catch.explanation: HTTP/3 keeps the same semantics as earlier versions. It uses QUIC instead of TCP.

card.text: HTTP/3 has the same semantics as earlier HTTP versions. But it uses QUIC instead of TCP for transport. QUIC runs many streams over UDP. In HTTP/2, one lost TCP packet can block all streams. In QUIC, each stream handles lost packets on its own. So a lost packet blocks only the stream with that data.
card.example: Your phone loads a page with many images on a weak network. One packet is lost. With HTTP/2, all images can wait. With HTTP/3, only the image in that packet waits.

review.question: Which transport protocol does QUIC run on?
review.answer: UDP. QUIC runs many streams over UDP.

screens.text: Transport Layer Security (TLS) lets a client talk to a server safely across an untrusted network. HTTP secured with TLS is called HTTPS. For example, https://example.com uses TLS.
TLS gives encryption: attackers cannot read the data while it travels. It also gives integrity: an attacker cannot secretly change the data without detection.

The third protection is authentication. Each side can prove to the other that it is who it claims to be. On the web, usually only the server proves its identity. So TLS hides data, detects changes and proves identity.

catch.question: HTTPS protects your shop's traffic with TLS. What does TLS give the connection?
choices: Encryption only, so nobody can read the data
Faster loading, because the data is compressed
A login check for every user of the site
catch.explanation: TLS encrypts the data, detects changes to it, and lets the server prove who it is. On the web, users usually do not authenticate with TLS.

card.text: TLS is a protocol for safe communication over an untrusted network. HTTP over TLS is called HTTPS. TLS gives three things. Encryption: an attacker cannot read the data in transit. Integrity: an attacker cannot secretly change the data. Authentication: each side can prove who it is. On the web, usually only the server proves its identity. HTTPS is the defense against a manipulator in the middle (MITM) attack.
card.example: You open https://example.com on public Wi-Fi. Another person on that network cannot read your password. They also cannot change the page without the browser noticing.

review.question: Which attack does HTTPS defend against?
review.answer: A manipulator in the middle (MITM) attack. The attacker sits between browser and server and reads or changes the traffic.

workedExample.problem: Your shop serves its login page at http://shop.example.com. A customer logs in on café Wi-Fi.
steps: Plain HTTP has no encryption.
Anyone on the same network can read the password.
An attacker can also change the page without detection.
TLS gives encryption, integrity and server authentication.
workedExample.answer: Serve every page and every subresource over HTTPS, with a valid certificate.

tradeOff.situation: Your shop serves only the login page over HTTPS. A teammate says the product pages hold no secrets, so HTTP is fine for them.
options: Use HTTPS for every page and subresource
Use HTTPS for only the login page
Use HTTPS for the login and cart pages only

reasons.text: Only pages with passwords are worth attacking, so other pages can stay on HTTP
A page without secrets cannot be harmed if an attacker changes it
A manipulator in the middle can read and change plain HTTP traffic. HTTPS defends against that on every page.

tradeOff.explanation: All pages and subresources should use HTTPS, because HTTPS is the defense against a manipulator in the middle. The cost is that you must set up a certificate and the server configuration.

decisionCards.situation: A partner system can only connect with TLS 1.0. Your security review says old TLS versions should go.
options: Keep TLS 1.0 on for the partner
Turn off TLS 1.0 and ask the partner to update

reasons.text: TLS 1.1 and TLS 1.0 should no longer be used. The current version is TLS 1.3.
All TLS versions give the same protection if the certificate is valid
Turning off a version breaks the handshake for every user, so never do it

decisionCards.explanation: TLS 1.1 and 1.0 should no longer be used, so the server should not allow them. The cost is that the partner cannot connect until it updates.

screens.text: When a client connects with TLS, it runs a handshake. First, client and server agree on which version of TLS to use.
Next, they agree on a cipher suite. It defines the algorithms for key agreement, authentication, encryption and message authentication. The server also proves who it is to the client.
The handshake also gives them a secret key. Client and server use that key to encrypt and decrypt messages. So the key is agreed first. Example: a visit to https://example.com/cart.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Version --> Cipher
  Cipher --> Identity
  Identity --> Key
  Key --> Messages

catch.question: When does TLS agree on the secret key for a connection?
choices: In the handshake, before any HTTP data is sent
After the first HTTP response arrives
Once a day, when the certificate is checked
Only when the user submits a form
catch.explanation: The handshake comes first. Then the key encrypts all messages, both headers and bodies.

card.text: When a client connects with TLS, a handshake comes first. Client and server agree on the TLS version. They agree on a cipher suite, the set of algorithms they will use. The server usually proves its identity. Last, they agree on a secret key. After the handshake, the key encrypts and decrypts every message.
card.example: Your browser opens https://example.com/cart. First the handshake runs. Then every HTTP header and the body travel encrypted.

review.question: After the TLS handshake, which parts of an HTTP message are encrypted?
review.answer: All of it, the HTTP headers as well as the body.

screens.text: Certificate authorities let browsers check who a website is, and then connect securely over TLS, that is, over HTTPS.
A certificate authority (CA) is an organization that signs digital certificates. A website certificate names at least the organization, the site and the certificate authority.
Browsers come with a list of root certificates. The browser checks that the site certificate was signed by a CA that chains back to a root. A signature from a trusted CA makes it genuine.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Root --> CA
  CA --> Certificate

catch.question: How does a browser know that a certificate for example.com is genuine?
choices: The server sends the certificate twice
The certificate is stored in a cookie
The domain owner signs the certificate with a password
A trusted certificate authority signed it
catch.explanation: A certificate authority signs the certificate. The browser checks that the signature chains back to a root certificate it already has.

card.text: A certificate authority (CA) is an organization that signs digital certificates and their public keys. A website certificate names at least the organization, the site, and the CA. Browsers come with a list of root certificates. The browser checks that the site certificate chains back to one of these roots. This lets the browser verify the website's identity.
card.example: You open https://example.com. The certificate says it is for example.com. A CA signed it. The signature chains back to a root certificate in your browser, so the browser accepts the site.

review.question: What does a certificate authority do?
review.answer: It signs digital certificates and their public keys. This says the information in them is correct.

screens.text: In the handshake, client and server agree on a TLS version. Your server configuration decides which TLS versions and algorithms can be used.
The current version is TLS 1.3, defined in RFC 8446. It is also the most widely used version. TLS 1.2 is still used by some websites.
TLS 1.1 and TLS 1.0 should no longer be used. So a server should not allow these old versions. Allow the current version, TLS 1.3, and turn off TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.

catch.question: Which TLS versions should a web server stop using?
choices: Only TLS 1.3, because it is too new
None, because all TLS versions are equal
catch.explanation: TLS 1.3 is the current version. TLS 1.1 and 1.0 should no longer be used.

card.text: In the handshake, client and server agree on a TLS version. The current version is TLS 1.3, defined in RFC 8446. It is also the most widely used version. Some websites still use TLS 1.2. TLS 1.1 and TLS 1.0 should no longer be used. Your server configuration decides which versions and algorithms are allowed.
card.example: You set up a new server for shop.example.com. Allow TLS 1.3. Turn off TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.

review.question: What is the current version of TLS?
review.answer: TLS 1.3, defined in RFC 8446.

screens.text: The Strict-Transport-Security header tells browsers that a host must be reached only with HTTPS. This is called HSTS. A server must send it over HTTPS only. Browsers ignore it over plain HTTP.
On later visits, the browser will not let the user bypass secure connection errors for that host. An invalid certificate is one example of such an error.
The browser remembers the header. Later, if the user opens an http URL for that host, the browser upgrades it to https by itself. Example header: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  User->>Browser: Opens an http URL
  Browser->>Server: Asks for the https URL instead

catch.question: A user types http://example.com after an earlier HTTPS visit. What makes the browser go straight to HTTPS?
choices: A 301 redirect sent on every request
The Strict-Transport-Security header from the earlier visit
The DNS cache from the earlier visit
A cookie that stores the word https
catch.explanation: The browser remembers the Strict-Transport-Security header. It then changes later http URLs to https before it sends anything.

card.text: The Strict-Transport-Security response header is often called HSTS. It tells the browser to use only HTTPS for this host. Later http URLs for the host become https automatically. The browser also blocks clicking through certificate errors for this host. Send the header over HTTPS only. Browsers ignore it over plain HTTP.
card.example: Your HTTPS response has this header: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains. Next week, the user opens http://example.com/cart. The browser requests https://example.com/cart instead.

review.question: Why do browsers ignore Strict-Transport-Security when it comes over plain HTTP?
review.answer: Over HTTP, a manipulator in the middle could change the header. So it only counts over HTTPS.

workedExample.problem: Your shop redirects http://shop.example.com to HTTPS with a 301. An attacker on public Wi-Fi stops that redirect.
steps: The first HTTP request is not protected, so an attacker can block the upgrade.
Strict-Transport-Security makes the browser use HTTPS directly on later visits.
workedExample.answer: Keep the 301 redirect, and send Strict-Transport-Security on every HTTPS response.

tradeOff.situation: Your shop redirects http to https with a 301. Security asks you to add the Strict-Transport-Security header too.
options: Keep only the 301 redirect
Keep the 301 and send the header on HTTPS responses only
Send the header on the http redirect response as well

reasons.text: The host must send the header over HTTPS only. Browsers then upgrade later http requests by themselves.
A 301 redirect already protects every visit, so the header adds nothing
The redirect is the first response, so it should carry the header

tradeOff.explanation: The header must come over HTTPS only, and browsers ignore it over HTTP. The cost is that the first http request stays open to attacks until the browser has seen the header.

decisionCards.situation: You want the first visit to be safe too. Your header today is Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000.
options: Only raise the max-age value
Add includeSubDomains and preload, and join the preload service

reasons.text: A longer max-age protects the first visit
Preloading mitigates the first-visit weakness, because browsers connect to your domain only via secure connections
The includeSubDomains directive alone protects the first visit

decisionCards.explanation: Preloading mitigates the first-visit weakness. The cost is that includeSubDomains must be present, so every subdomain falls under the policy.

screens.text: Look at this header: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000. The max-age value is a time in seconds. The browser remembers for that long that the host is HTTPS-only. 31536000 seconds is one year.
Each time the browser gets the header, it adds max-age to the current time again. So the timer starts over on every response.
The optional includeSubDomains directive applies the policy to all subdomains too. To turn HSTS off, send max-age=0. This takes effect only after the browser gets it over HTTPS.

catch.question: In Strict-Transport-Security, what does max-age=31536000 mean?
choices: The certificate is valid for 31536000 days
The page can be cached for one year
The browser remembers HTTPS-only for 31536000 seconds
catch.explanation: max-age is in seconds. 31536000 seconds is one year.

card.text: max-age is the time, in seconds, that the browser remembers to use only HTTPS. Each new header adds max-age to the current time again. The optional includeSubDomains directive applies the rule to all subdomains too. It covers names under the host, not the parent domain. To turn HSTS off, send max-age=0 over HTTPS.
card.example: secure.example.com sends Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains. The rule also covers login.secure.example.com. It does not cover example.com.

review.question: How do you turn HSTS off for your host?
review.answer: Send Strict-Transport-Security with max-age=0 over HTTPS. You cannot turn it off over plain HTTP.

screens.text: HSTS has one weakness. It does not work until the browser has made one secure connection and received the header. The first http request is open to network attacks.
Preloading mitigates this problem. Google maintains an HSTS preload service. After you submit your domain, browsers connect to it only via secure connections.

Preload has rules. The max-age must be at least 31536000, which is one year. The includeSubDomains directive must be present. Example: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload.

catch.question: HSTS only works after one HTTPS visit. What protects the very first visit?
choices: The HSTS preload list built into browsers
catch.explanation: Browsers ship with a preload list of HSTS domains. A listed domain uses HTTPS even on the first visit.

card.text: HSTS has one weakness. It works only after the browser gets the header once over HTTPS. So the very first http request is open to attacks. Preloading fixes this. Google runs an HSTS preload service, and all browsers use its list. Its rules include a max-age of at least 31536000, which is one year. The header also needs includeSubDomains and preload.
card.example: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload. This header sets two years and can join the preload list.

review.question: What is the smallest max-age a domain needs for the HSTS preload list?
review.answer: 31536000 seconds, which is one year. The header also needs includeSubDomains and preload.

screens.text: A page loaded over HTTPS is secure. The browser wants every resource on that page to be secure too. A resource is a script, an image, a style file and so on.
Mixed content is a secure page that fetches a resource over HTTP or another insecure protocol. An attacker can read that resource on its way. The attacker may also change it.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Secure page] --> B[HTTP resource]
  B --> C[Attacker can read or change it]

screens.text: Example: https://shop.example.com loads http://cdn.example.com/logo.png. This is mixed content. The best fix is to serve all content over HTTPS. Use https links or relative links.

catch.question: Your page loads over HTTPS, but one script loads from an http URL. What is this called?
catch.explanation: A secure page that fetches resources over HTTP has mixed content. Those resources lose the protection of HTTPS.

card.text: Mixed content is a page loaded over HTTPS that fetches resources over HTTP. Those resources do not get HTTPS protection. An attacker can read them and maybe change them. Mixed content has two groups. Browsers upgrade upgradable content to HTTPS. Browsers block blockable content. The best fix is to serve all content over HTTPS.
card.example: https://shop.example.com loads http://cdn.example.com/logo.png. This is mixed content. http://old.example.com loads http://cdn.example.com/logo.png. This is not mixed content, because both are insecure.

review.question: Why is mixed content unsafe?
review.answer: The HTTP resources do not get HTTPS protection. An attacker can read them and maybe change them.

workedExample.problem: Your shop moved to https://shop.example.com. The menu stops working, and the console shows mixed content warnings.
steps: The console names the URLs that still use http.
One is a script at http://shop.example.com/menu.js.
Scripts are blockable content, so the browser blocked it.
workedExample.answer: Change the script URL to https or to a relative link. Do the same for every other http URL.

tradeOff.situation: Your shop moves to HTTPS. The console lists many http URLs, and the menu script is blocked.
options: Keep the http URLs, because browsers upgrade all mixed content
Change every http URL to https or a relative link, then check the console
Keep the http scripts and only fix the images

reasons.text: Browsers upgrade every kind of mixed content, so nothing needs a change.
Images are harmless, so only scripts matter.
The best strategy is to serve all content over HTTPS, so every link must be secure.

tradeOff.explanation: Serving all content over HTTPS removes the risk for scripts and images. It costs time: you must check every link, and each third party needs an https version.

decisionCards.situation: Your HTTPS page has a script at http://cdn.example.com/menu.js. The browser blocks it and the menu breaks.
options: Tell users to allow mixed content in their browser
Change the script URL to https or a relative link

reasons.text: The browser will upgrade the script to https by itself soon.
A script can change any part of the page, so it must load over HTTPS.
Blocking a script is a browser bug, so users should switch it off.

decisionCards.explanation: A script can change any part of the page, so you must fix the URL. The cost is a code change and a new deploy.

screens.text: Some mixed content is easy for the browser to repair. The browser has two ways to handle mixed content: upgrade it or block it. This move is about the upgrade.
Upgradable content is repaired by the browser. It changes the scheme from http to https by itself. Images, audio and video with a src are in this group.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Page asks for an http image] --> B[Browser upgrades it]
  B --> C[https request]

screens.text: Example: your HTTPS page has a video with src http://example.com/demo.mp4. The browser requests https://example.com/demo.mp4. But if the host is an IP address, the browser blocks the request instead.

catch.question: An HTTPS page has . What should a current browser do?
choices: Block the image and show a broken icon
Load the image over HTTP with no change
Ask the user to allow the image
Change the URL to https and load it
catch.explanation: An img with src is upgradable content. The browser changes the scheme from http to https.

card.text: Upgradable content is mixed content that the browser fixes by itself. The browser changes the scheme from http to https. Upgradable content includes with src,
card.example: Your HTTPS page has <video src="http://example.com/demo.mp4">. The browser requests https://example.com/demo.mp4 instead.

review.question: What does a browser do with upgradable mixed content?
review.answer: It changes the request scheme from http to https automatically.

screens.text: Not all mixed content can be upgraded. The browser has no safe automatic repair for some of it. For those requests, it does something else.
Blockable content is all mixed content that is not upgradable. The browser blocks the request. Scripts, stylesheets, iframes, fetch and XMLHttpRequest calls are in this group.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[HTTPS page] --> B[fetch to an http URL]
  B --> C[Browser blocks it]

screens.text: Example: your HTTPS page has a script with src http://example.com/menu.js. The browser blocks the script, so the menu does not work. A fetch to an http URL is blocked in the same way.

catch.question: An HTTPS page calls fetch("http://api.example.com/cart"). What happens?
choices: The browser upgrades it to https
The request works, but without cookies
The browser sends a preflight first
catch.explanation: fetch() is blockable content. The browser blocks the insecure request.

card.text: Blockable content is all mixed content that is not upgradable. Browsers block these requests. Examples are <script> with src and <link> with href, including stylesheets. Also <iframe> with src, fetch() and XMLHttpRequest. Web fonts and images set with srcset or <picture> are blockable too.
card.example: Your HTTPS page has <script src="http://example.com/menu.js"></script>. The browser blocks the script, so the menu does not work.

review.question: Name two kinds of blockable mixed content.
review.answer: For example, a <script> with an http src, and a fetch() call to an http URL.

screens.text: The same-origin policy limits how a script from one origin can use a resource from another origin. It helps to isolate documents that may be harmful.
Cross-origin actions fall in three groups. Writes, like links and form submissions, are typically allowed. Embedding, like images and scripts, is typically allowed. Reads are typically not allowed.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Shop script] --> B[Browser]
  B --> C[Read blocked]

screens.text: Example: a page on https://shop.example.com shows an image from https://cdn.example.net. This works. But its script cannot read a fetch response from there. The server must use CORS to allow it.

catch.question: A script on https://shop.example.com fetches JSON from https://api.example.net. By default, what can the script do?
choices: It can read the response, because both use HTTPS
It can read the response, but not the headers
It cannot even start the request
catch.explanation: The two URLs have different hosts, so they are different origins. Cross-origin reads are typically not allowed.

card.text: The same-origin policy controls how two different origins interact. Cross-origin writes, like links, redirects and form submissions, are typically allowed. Cross-origin embedding, like or
card.example: Your page on https://shop.example.com shows . This works. But your script cannot read a fetch() response from https://cdn.example.net without CORS.

review.question: What does a server use to allow cross-origin access?
review.answer: CORS. It is a part of HTTP that lets servers say which other hosts may load their content.

workedExample.problem: Your web app at https://app.example.com calls fetch() on https://api.example.com. The code gets an error, not the data.
steps: Compare scheme, host and port of both URLs.
The hosts differ: app.example.com and api.example.com.
So these are two origins, and cross-origin reads are blocked by default.
workedExample.answer: Let the API allow the app's origin with CORS headers.

tradeOff.situation: Your site serves a private image. You want other sites to learn nothing about it, not even its size.
options: Rely on the same-origin policy alone, because it blocks every cross-origin read
Send Access-Control-Allow-Origin with a star on the image response
Make sure other sites cannot embed the image

reasons.text: Embedding a resource always leaks some information about it, even when reads are blocked.
The same-origin policy blocks every cross-origin action, including embedding.
A star in CORS keeps a resource private from other origins.

tradeOff.explanation: Embedding always leaks some information, such as the size of an image, so the policy alone is not enough. The cost is that no other site can show this image.

decisionCards.situation: A form on https://shop.example.com posts to https://pay.example.net. Do you need CORS for the form to be sent?
options: Yes, the server must send CORS headers first
No, cross-origin form submissions are typically allowed

reasons.text: Every cross-origin request is blocked until the server opts in.
Cross-origin writes, like form submissions, are typically allowed.
Forms are embedding, and embedding is blocked by default.

decisionCards.explanation: Cross-origin writes such as form submissions are typically allowed. The cost is that a script on the shop page still cannot read the answer without CORS.

screens.text: The browser checks three parts of a URL to decide its origin. These parts are the protocol, the host and the port.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Protocol --> Host
  Host --> Port
  Port --> Origin

screens.text: Two URLs have the same origin when the protocol, host and port are all equal. The path does not count. For http, the default port is 80.

Compare with http://store.example.com/dir/page.html. Same origin: http://store.example.com/dir2/other.html, because only the path changed. Different origin: https at the start, port 81, or the host news.example.com.

catch.question: Which URL has the same origin as http://store.example.com/dir/page.html?
catch.explanation: Only the path is different, and the path is not part of the origin. The other URLs change the protocol, port or host.

card.text: Two URLs have the same origin when the protocol, host and port are the same. People also call this the scheme/host/port tuple. The path does not count. http:// uses port 80 by default.
card.example: Compare with http://store.example.com/dir/page.html. Same origin: http://store.example.com/dir2/other.html. Different: https://store.example.com/page.html, because the protocol differs. Different: http://store.example.com:81/dir/page.html, because the port differs. Different: http://news.example.com/dir/page.html, because the host differs.

review.question: Which three parts of a URL make its origin?
review.answer: The protocol (scheme), the host and the port.

screens.text: The same-origin policy sorts cross-origin actions into three groups: writes, embedding and reads. The browser treats each group in its own way.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Write --> Allowed
  Embed --> Allowed
  Read --> Blocked

screens.text: Writes are typically allowed: links, redirects and form submissions. Embedding is typically allowed too: images, scripts, video and iframes.

Reads are typically not allowed. A script cannot read a response from another origin. Example: a form on https://shop.example.com posts to https://pay.example.net, which works. A fetch response from there cannot be read.

catch.question: Which cross-origin action does the same-origin policy typically block?
choices: A link to a page on another origin
A form submission to another origin
An tag that shows an image from another origin
A script that reads a response from another origin
catch.explanation: Writes like links and form submissions are typically allowed. Embedding is typically allowed. Reads are typically blocked.

card.text: The same-origin policy puts cross-origin actions into three groups. Writes are typically allowed: links, redirects and form submissions. Embedding is typically allowed:
card.example: A form on https://shop.example.com posts to https://pay.example.net. This is allowed. A script on the shop page tries to read a fetch() response from https://pay.example.net. This is blocked.

review.question: Give one example of a cross-origin write that is typically allowed.
review.answer: A link, a redirect or a form submission to another origin.

screens.text: By default, fetch and XMLHttpRequest follow the same-origin policy. A script cannot read a response from another origin. The server must allow it.
CORS means Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. It is based on HTTP headers. The server tells the browser which other origins may load its resources. So the server must change, not the user.
Example: a page on https://foo.example sends a GET to https://bar.other with the header Origin: https://foo.example. The response has Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. So the page can read it.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>API: GET with an Origin header
  API-->>Browser: Access-Control-Allow-Origin header

catch.question: Your front end on another origin cannot read your API's response. Who must change something to allow it?
choices: The browser user, in the browser settings
The API server, by sending CORS headers
The front end, by adding a cookie
Nobody, because HTTPS allows it already
catch.explanation: CORS is header based. The server says which other origins may read its responses.

card.text: CORS means Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. It is an HTTP-header based mechanism. With it, a server tells the browser which other origins may load its resources. fetch() and XMLHttpRequest follow the same-origin policy. They can read a response from another origin only with the right CORS headers. When CORS fails, JavaScript sees only that an error happened. The browser console shows the details.
card.example: A page on https://foo.example sends a GET to https://bar.other with the header Origin: https://foo.example. The response has Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. So the page can read it.

review.question: Where can you see the details of a CORS error?
review.answer: In the browser console. JavaScript only learns that an error happened.

workedExample.problem: Your shop front end on https://shop.example.com calls https://api.example.com/products. The console shows a CORS error.
steps: The two URLs have different hosts, so they are different origins.
The browser lets the page read the response only with the right CORS headers.
The API response has no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header.
workedExample.answer: Make the API send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://shop.example.com. Also send Vary: Origin.

tradeOff.situation: Your front end sends JSON with PUT to your API many times each minute. Each call starts with a preflight request.
options: Send Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400 on the preflight response
Change the API so it accepts only GET
Send Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the real response only

reasons.text: The browser can keep the preflight answer, so it sends fewer preflight requests.
With Max-Age the server no longer needs to answer OPTIONS at all.
Preflight is only needed for old browsers, so you can switch it off.

tradeOff.explanation: Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser keep the preflight answer, so there are fewer extra requests. The cost is that each browser has its own maximum, so the cache time may be shorter.

decisionCards.situation: Your front end gets a CORS error. The JavaScript code only learns that an error happened.
options: Look in the browser console for the details
Read the JavaScript error object for the failed header

reasons.text: For security, the browser does not give the details to JavaScript.
The JavaScript error object always names the missing header.
The server log always shows the reason the browser gave.

decisionCards.explanation: The browser hides the details from JavaScript, but the console shows them. The cost is that your code cannot show users the exact cause.

screens.text: Access-Control-Allow-Origin says which origin may read a response. The value is one origin, or a star for any origin.
If you name one origin, also send Vary: Origin. This tells clients that the response depends on the Origin request header.
Example: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://mozilla.org together with Vary: Origin. Only pages from https://mozilla.org can read this response. A star works only for requests without credentials.

catch.question: Your API allows only one origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Which other header should it also send?
catch.explanation: Vary: Origin tells clients that the response changes with the Origin request header.

card.text: Access-Control-Allow-Origin names the origin that may read the response. The value is one origin, or * for any origin. The * wildcard works only for requests without credentials. If you name one origin, also send Vary: Origin. This says the response depends on the Origin request header.
card.example: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://mozilla.org. Vary: Origin. Only pages from https://mozilla.org can read this response.

review.question: What does Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * mean?
review.answer: Any origin can read the resource. It only works for requests without credentials.

screens.text: Some cross-origin requests need no preflight. The browser calls them simple requests. The server still must send Access-Control-Allow-Origin so the script can read the response.
A simple request uses GET, HEAD or POST. It sets only safelisted headers. Content-Type must be application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain.
Example: a POST with Content-Type text/plain and no custom headers is simple. A POST with Content-Type application/json is not, so the browser sends a preflight first.

catch.question: Which cross-origin fetch() is a simple request, with no preflight?
choices: GET with a custom header X-Shop-Token
catch.explanation: A simple request uses GET, HEAD or POST, safelisted headers, and one of three Content-Type values. application/x-www-form-urlencoded is one of them.

card.text: A simple request needs no preflight. These are its main rules. The method is GET, HEAD or POST. You set only CORS-safelisted headers, such as Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Language and Content-Type. Content-Type is only application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain. No ReadableStream is used in the request.
card.example: A POST with Content-Type: text/plain and no custom headers is a simple request. A POST with Content-Type: application/json is not, so the browser sends a preflight first.

review.question: Which three methods can a simple request use?
review.answer: GET, HEAD and POST.

screens.text: Before a request that is not simple, the browser asks first. A PUT is one example. This first request is called a preflight. It checks if the real request is safe to send.
The preflight uses the OPTIONS method. It names the real method in Access-Control-Request-Method. The server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers.

Example: OPTIONS /doc with Access-Control-Request-Method: POST. The answer is 204 No Content with Access-Control-Allow-Methods: POST, GET, OPTIONS. Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400 lets the browser keep this answer for 24 hours.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Browser->>API: OPTIONS /doc
  API-->>Browser: 204 No Content
  Browser->>API: the real request

catch.question: Before a cross-origin PUT, the browser sends a request first. Which method does that first request use?
catch.explanation: The preflight uses OPTIONS. It asks the server if the real request is allowed.

card.text: For a request that is not simple, the browser first sends a preflight. It is an OPTIONS request to the other origin. It asks if the actual request is safe to send. Access-Control-Request-Method names the method of the actual request. Access-Control-Request-Headers names its extra headers. The server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers.
card.example: Request: OPTIONS /doc with Access-Control-Request-Method: POST. Response: 204 No Content with Access-Control-Allow-Methods: POST, GET, OPTIONS. Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400 lets the browser keep this answer for 24 hours.

review.question: In a preflight, which header tells the server the method of the actual request?
review.answer: Access-Control-Request-Method, for example Access-Control-Request-Method: POST.

screens.text: By default, a cross-origin fetch does not send credentials such as cookies. To send them, set credentials to include.

Then the server must send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. It must also name one exact origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, not a star. Otherwise the browser blocks the response and reports a CORS error.

Example: a fetch with credentials include from https://foo.example. The response has Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://foo.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Now the page can read it. A preflight never carries credentials.

catch.question: A cross-origin fetch() uses credentials: "include". The response has Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. What happens?
choices: The browser blocks access to the response
The page reads the response normally
The server gets no request at all
catch.explanation: With credentials, the * wildcard is not allowed. The browser blocks the response and reports a CORS error.

card.text: By default, cross-origin fetch() does not send credentials such as cookies. To send them, set credentials to "include". The response needs Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Access-Control-Allow-Origin must name an exact origin, not *. Otherwise the browser blocks the response. Preflight requests never carry credentials.
card.example: Request: fetch(url, { credentials: "include" }) from https://foo.example. Response: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://foo.example. Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Now the page can read the response.

review.question: Which response header must be true for a credentialed cross-origin response?
review.answer: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

placement.question: In HTTP, can the server send a message before the client asks?
placement.answer: No. The client always starts the request, and the server answers.

placement.question: What separates the headers from the body in an HTTP/1.1 message?
placement.answer: An empty line.

placement.question: Which HTTP method asks only to get data?
placement.answer: GET. A GET request should only retrieve data.

placement.question: What does a 3xx status code mean, and which header goes with it?
placement.answer: It is a redirect. The Location header holds the new URL.

placement.question: What is the MIME type for JSON data?
placement.answer: application/json.

placement.question: Does HTTP itself link two requests from the same user?
placement.answer: No. HTTP is stateless, and cookies add a session on top.

placement.question: Which header does a server use to store a cookie in the browser?
placement.answer: Set-Cookie. The browser sends the cookie back in the Cookie header.

placement.question: Name two jobs a proxy can do between a client and a server.
placement.answer: For example caching and filtering, or load balancing and logging.

placement.question: What does DNS do before your browser connects to a site?
placement.answer: It turns the domain name into an IP address.

placement.question: What does HTTP/3 use instead of TCP?
placement.answer: QUIC, which runs over UDP.

scenarios.name: The empty sign-up
scenarios.problem: New sign-ups arrive empty or wrong. You use an HTTP network monitor to read the raw messages.

turns.threat: The form posts a name and an email, but the server saves an empty user.
turns.constraint: The network monitor shows that the request uses the POST method, as planned.

reasons.text: A POST form sends its data in the body.
The form fields travel in the request line, next to the method and the URL.
Another browser may send the form data that this one dropped.

moves.counterattack: You confirm the method is POST, but a POST form sends its data in the body.
You find the empty body, but you still must find the code that dropped the data.
You read the server's reply, but the data was lost in the request.
You switch the user agent to a debugging program, but the form bug is still there.

turns.modelAnswer: A POST form sends its data in the request body, after the headers and one empty line. Check that the body is there. Reading raw messages takes time, but it shows what was really sent.
keyPoints: A POST form sends its data in the request body.
The body comes after the headers and an empty line.
The raw message shows what was really sent.

turns.threat: The server now rejects bad emails, but the app shows Welcome for every sign-up.
turns.constraint: Each response has a status code, and the error text in the body changes often.

reasons.text: The reason phrase in the status line is what tells the app it failed.
A reply that has a body means the server accepted the request.
The status code says if the request worked, and it does not change with releases.

moves.counterattack: You look at the servers behind the address, but the app still ignores the reply.
The app reads the error text in the body, but it must guess what each text means.
The request line is correct, so the wrong Welcome screen stays.
The app reads the status code now, but you must write a message for each failure.

turns.modelAnswer: Read the status line of the response. Its status code says if the request succeeded or failed. The reason phrase is only text for humans. The cost: the app needs a message for each failure code.
keyPoints: The status line is the first line of the response.
The status code says success or failure.
The reason phrase is optional text for humans.

turns.threat: Each refresh of the profile page shows different data. Support thinks users lost their data.
turns.constraint: The site looks like one machine, but the host runs three servers behind it.

reasons.text: A different answer on each refresh points to a broken browser cache.
One address can hide many servers that share the load.
Users lost data, so the database deleted rows.

moves.counterattack: You find three servers behind one address, but now each one must give the same data.
Every reply says 200 OK, so the status line hides the problem.
You test in another browser, but the data still changes on each refresh.
You see the bodies differ, but you still do not know which machine sent each one.

turns.modelAnswer: One server address can hide many servers that share the load. Each refresh can reach a different one. Find the server that gives different data. The cost: every server must now serve the same data.
keyPoints: One address can be many servers.
Load balancing sends each request to one of them.
Every server behind the address must give the same data.

scenarios.name: Live prices
scenarios.problem: The product manager wants open pages to show new prices at once. The site uses plain HTTP.

turns.threat: The plan says the server sends each new price to every open page by itself.
turns.constraint: The site must keep plain HTTP requests and responses, with no new protocol.

reasons.text: In HTTP, the client starts every request, so the page must ask for the price.
A server can send a response by itself as soon as its data changes.
With enough servers, HTTP can send a message to the browser first.

moves.counterattack: You add servers to send prices, but in plain HTTP no server starts a message.
You plan a new status code for prices, but the server still cannot send first.
The page now asks for prices itself, but each check is one more request.
You put the price in a response body, but the browser must still ask for it.

turns.modelAnswer: In HTTP, the browser always starts the request, never the server. So the page must ask for the new price. The cost: more requests reach the server.
keyPoints: The client always starts the request.
The server only answers requests.
Asking again means more requests to the server.

turns.threat: A teammate builds the price check as POST /price, because it runs every few seconds.
turns.constraint: The price check runs every few seconds and never changes data.

reasons.text: POST fits better for a request that runs every few seconds.
The method name matters little when the server code changes nothing.
A read-only request should use a safe method like GET.

moves.counterattack: POST stays, so each price check looks like a request that may change the server.
You see POST in the request line, but you have not picked a better method yet.
The check becomes a read-only GET, but the server code must really change nothing.

turns.modelAnswer: Reading a price does not change the server, so use GET, a safe method. Safe methods are read-only in meaning. The cost: the server code must keep GET free of changes.
keyPoints: Reading a price is a read-only action.
GET is a safe method.
The server code must keep GET free of changes.

turns.threat: The price GET sends the product id in a JSON body. Some servers drop it.
turns.constraint: The product id is not secret, so it can appear in the URL.

reasons.text: A GET body reaches the server like a POST body.
A GET body can be dropped, so the id goes in the URL.
POST is a safe choice here, because the price check changes nothing.

moves.counterattack: The id moves into the URL as /price?product=42, but every caller must change its URL.
You move the id into a custom header, but the URL query is the usual place for it.
You switch back to POST to keep the body, so the check is no longer safe.
GET is idempotent, but the body is still dropped on some servers.

turns.modelAnswer: Only PATCH, POST and PUT requests have a body, so a GET body can get lost. Put the product id in the request target, for example GET /price?product=42. The cost: every caller must change its URL.
keyPoints: Only PATCH, POST and PUT requests have a body.
The request target can carry a query string.
Every caller must change to the new URL.

scenarios.name: The crawler deletes posts
scenarios.problem: Blog posts disappear at night. The logs show a web crawler on the admin pages.

turns.threat: Each admin page has links like GET /posts/7/delete. The crawler follows every link.
turns.constraint: The delete action runs on a GET link, and spiders follow such links.

reasons.text: The sign-in check keeps programs that follow links out of the admin pages.
Deleting a post twice does no harm.
A GET must not change data, because spiders follow links.

moves.counterattack: Delete moves off GET, but every delete link must become a button or a form.
Deleting twice has the same effect, but the crawler still deletes each post once.
You see GET in the request line, but the posts still disappear.
You learn the crawler is a user agent too, but it keeps deleting posts.

turns.modelAnswer: Crawlers call safe methods, because safe methods should not change the server's state. A GET that deletes breaks this rule. Move the delete off GET. The cost: every delete link needs a new button or form.
keyPoints: Crawlers and browsers call safe methods freely.
GET should not change the server's state.
Every delete link must change.

turns.threat: The new delete uses DELETE /posts/7. On a slow network the admin app sends it twice.
turns.constraint: The app cannot tell if the first DELETE arrived before the communication failed.

reasons.text: DELETE is idempotent, so a repeat has the same intended effect as one call.
Only methods that change nothing on the server are safe to send again.
POST is safer to repeat, because each call is a new request.

moves.counterattack: You switch to POST, which is not idempotent, so a second call can act again.
You see two different status codes, but you cannot explain them yet.
The second DELETE has no new effect, but the app must accept a 404 reply.
You call DELETE safe, but it changes the server, so the review misses the risk.

turns.modelAnswer: DELETE is idempotent. Two identical calls have the same intended effect as one, so a retry does no harm. The cost: the second call can return 404.
keyPoints: DELETE is idempotent.
A retry of DELETE does no extra harm.
The second reply can be 404.

turns.threat: Admins create posts with POST /posts. The slow network sends that request twice too.
turns.constraint: The app retries every request by itself after a communication failure.

reasons.text: Once DELETE is safe to retry, the other write methods are safe to retry too.
POST is not idempotent, so a retry can create a second post.
The server sees the same body twice and keeps only one post.

moves.counterattack: You treat POST like DELETE, so the retry creates a second post.
The second request has the same body, so the server creates the same post again.
The app stops blind retries of POST, but admins must check for a lost post.

turns.modelAnswer: POST is not idempotent. Identical POST requests may create the same item twice. Do not resend it blindly. The cost: after a lost reply, the admin must check the post list.
keyPoints: POST is not safe and not idempotent.
A repeated POST can create a second post.
The app must not resend POST blindly.

scenarios.name: Confusing account errors
scenarios.problem: Customers complain about the account pages. The API answers with the wrong status codes.

turns.threat: A customer who is not signed in opens /account and gets 403 Forbidden.
turns.constraint: Mobile apps call /account directly and must know when the user has to sign in.

reasons.text: 403 fits any customer who has no access to the account page yet.
401 means unauthenticated: the client must sign in to get the response.
A redirect to the sign-in page works for mobile apps too.

moves.counterattack: You return 500, so monitoring shows a server crash that did not happen.
You redirect strangers to the sign-in page, but API clients still get no clear 401.
You change the reason phrase, but the code is still 403.
The API sends 401 to strangers now, but the app must show a sign-in step for it.

turns.modelAnswer: 401 really means unauthenticated: the client must prove who it is. 403 means the server knows the client, but it has no rights. Send 401 here. The cost: the app needs a sign-in step for 401.
keyPoints: 401 means the client must sign in.
403 means the client is known but has no rights.
The app must answer 401 with a sign-in step.

turns.threat: The sign-up API answers 200 OK with an empty body. The app cannot find the new user.
turns.constraint: Every app that uses the sign-up API can be updated this week.

reasons.text: 200 OK says the new user exists.
Sending the POST again is a quick way to read the new user.
201 Created says a new resource was made.

moves.counterattack: The API now sends 201 Created, but old apps still expect 200.
You redirect to the new user page, but each sign-up now makes one more request.
You put the user in the body, but the code still does not say a user was created.
You resend the POST to get the data, so a second user is created.

turns.modelAnswer: 201 Created says the request succeeded and made a new resource. Servers typically send it after POST. The cost: old apps that expect 200 must change.
keyPoints: 201 Created means a new resource was made.
It typically answers a POST.
Old apps that expect 200 must change.

turns.threat: During tonight's database work, the API will answer 500 Internal Server Error for one hour.
turns.constraint: The database work is planned maintenance, and it ends in about one hour.

reasons.text: 503 means temporary, and Retry-After says when to return.
A 200 page with a friendly error text keeps clients calm.
A 400 code makes clients stop for a while.

moves.counterattack: You send 400, so clients think their own requests are wrong.
Clients get 503 with a Retry-After time, but you should usually keep that reply out of caches.
You send 200 with an error text, so monitoring sees no problem at all.
You redirect to a status page, but API clients get no clear error code.

turns.modelAnswer: Use 503 Service Unavailable for maintenance. It is meant for temporary conditions. Add Retry-After with the expected recovery time. The cost: the 503 reply should usually not be cached.
keyPoints: 503 means the server is not ready for now.
Retry-After tells clients when to come back.
Temporary error replies should usually not be cached.

scenarios.name: The moved shop

source.title: Google Search Central: Site moves with URL changes

scenarios.problem: Your shop moves all product pages to new URLs. Many other sites still link to the old ones.

turns.threat: Next week the old URLs will answer 404 Not Found. Search engines and bookmarks still use them.
turns.constraint: The move is permanent, and most visits come from search results.

reasons.text: A 301 tells browsers and search engines the new URL.
Two URLs for one page is fine, because search engines pick the best one.
A 404 page with a link to the new page works as well as a redirect.

moves.counterattack: 404 says the server cannot find the page, so old links and search visits break.
You serve each page on both URLs, but every page now has two locations.
Old URLs answer 301 with the new Location, but each old link costs one extra request.

turns.modelAnswer: Answer the old URLs with 301 Moved Permanently and a Location header. Browsers load the new URL at once, and search engines update the old one. The cost: one extra round trip.
keyPoints: 301 means the move is permanent.
The Location header holds the new URL.
Each redirect costs one extra request.

turns.threat: Some old products are gone for good. Their old URLs now redirect to the home page.
turns.constraint: The gone products have no replacement in the new shop.

reasons.text: Sending old links to the home page keeps visitors in the shop.
The home page answers 200, so nothing looks broken.
A page gone for good should answer with a 4xx code, like 410 Gone.

moves.counterattack: The home page answers 200, so shoppers on old links never learn the product is gone.
Old links still land on the home page, so shoppers still look for the product.
You send 500, so monitoring reports a crash that did not happen.
Gone products answer 410 Gone, but shoppers on old links see an error page.

turns.modelAnswer: When a product is gone for good, answer with a 4xx client error. 410 Gone means the content was deleted for good. 404 means the server cannot find it. The cost: shoppers on old links see an error page.
keyPoints: A gone product gets a 4xx client error.
410 Gone means the content was deleted for good.
Shoppers on old links now see an error page.

turns.threat: After a config change for the redirects, every new URL answers 500 Internal Server Error.
turns.constraint: The server error logs show the 500 errors began when the new redirects went live.

reasons.text: A 500 error comes from the shopper's browser.
A 5xx code means the server failed, so check its last change.
The error body names the fault, so read it before you change anything.

moves.counterattack: You clear your own browser data, but every visitor still sees the error.
You check the new server config, find the mistake, and roll the change back.
You check the shoppers' requests, but the error comes from the server.
You read the error body, but it only says something went wrong.

turns.modelAnswer: 5xx codes are server errors, and 500 is the generic one. So look first at what changed on the server, like the new redirect config. The cost: you roll the change back while you fix it.
keyPoints: 5xx means the server failed, not the client.
500 is a generic server error.
Check the last change on the server first.

scenarios.name: Broken styles
scenarios.problem: After a move to a new server, the shop shows plain text with no design. All files are there.

turns.threat: The new server sends style.css with Content-Type: text/plain, and browsers ignore the styles.
turns.constraint: The server also sends X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so browsers do not guess the type.

reasons.text: A file named style.css is read as CSS, whatever the server says.
Browsers use the MIME type, not the file extension.
The Accept header of the browser decides how it reads the file.

moves.counterattack: You tune the Accept header, but the server still labels the CSS as text/plain.
You find the wrong header line, but you do not know the right value yet.
The file already answers 200 OK, so the status code is not the problem.
The server sends text/css now, but you must check every other file type too.

turns.modelAnswer: Browsers use the MIME type, not the file extension. CSS must be sent as text/css, or most browsers ignore it. Fix the server config. The cost: you must check every file type it serves.
keyPoints: Browsers trust the MIME type, not the file extension.
CSS must be sent as text/css.
Check the types of all served files.

turns.threat: Product photo uploads now fail with 415 Unsupported Media Type.
turns.constraint: The upload form sends a photo file together with a text field.

reasons.text: A form with files is sent as multipart/form-data, with that type in Content-Type.
A 415 error means the server is overloaded, so a restart should help.
The Accept header tells the server what kind of body the client sends.

moves.counterattack: The upload sends multipart/form-data now, but every upload client must send it.
You read 415 as a client error and check the request, but not yet its type.
You change the Accept header, but it only says what the client can read.
You restart the server, but it still rejects the photos.

turns.modelAnswer: In a POST, the Content-Type header says the type of the request body. Forms with files use multipart/form-data. The cost: every upload client must send it.
keyPoints: Content-Type in a request says the body's type.
A form with files is sent as multipart/form-data.
Every upload client must send the new type.

turns.threat: The mobile app asks for product data and gets an HTML page instead of JSON.
turns.constraint: The API can send application/json to apps and HTML pages to browsers.

reasons.text: The Content-Type of a GET request tells the server what to send back.
The server tells apps apart by the method.
The client names the type it wants in Accept.

moves.counterattack: You see the reply says text/html, but the app still asks for the same thing.
The app sends Accept: application/json now, but the server must keep both formats working.
You test in a browser, but the browser also asks for HTML first.
The GET is already safe, so the reply is still HTML.

turns.modelAnswer: The client lists the types it understands in the Accept header. The server picks one and names it in Content-Type. Ask for application/json. The cost: the server must keep each format it offers working.
keyPoints: Accept lists the types the client can read.
The server picks one and names it in Content-Type.
The server must support each type it offers.

scenarios.name: The lost cart
scenarios.problem: Shoppers add items, but the cart page is often empty. The shop runs on plain HTTP requests.

turns.threat: The add-to-cart request and the cart page request share nothing that links them.
turns.constraint: Shoppers do not sign in before they add items, and the server can store carts.

reasons.text: Keeping one connection open links the requests of one shopper.
The page body can carry the cart.
A session cookie links separate requests to one cart.

moves.counterattack: You keep one connection open, but HTTP still has no link between the requests.
You see that HTTP has no link between requests, but the cart is still empty.
Each request carries a session cookie now, but the server must store every cart.
You put the cart in the page body, but the next request forgets it.

turns.modelAnswer: HTTP is stateless, even on one connection. A cookie adds a session on top of it. Each request carries the cookie, so the server finds the cart. The cost: the server must store every cart.
keyPoints: HTTP has no link between two requests.
A session cookie links the requests.
The server must keep each session's state.

turns.threat: Shoppers close the browser at lunch. In the evening, their cart is gone.
turns.constraint: Most shoppers use their own phone or laptop.

reasons.text: A cookie without Expires or Max-Age ends with the session.
Sending the same Set-Cookie on every page makes the cookie last longer.
The Secure and HttpOnly flags also decide how long the cookie lives.

moves.counterattack: You send the same Set-Cookie again, but it still ends when the browser closes.
The cookie is safer now, but it still ends with the session.
You explain that HTTP has no memory, but the cart is still lost.
The cart cookie has a Max-Age of 30 days now, so it stays on that browser longer.

turns.modelAnswer: A cookie with no Expires and no Max-Age is a session cookie. The browser removes it when the session ends. Give the cart cookie a Max-Age. The cost: the cookie stays on the device longer.
keyPoints: A session cookie has no Expires and no Max-Age.
Max-Age keeps the cookie for a set time.
A longer lifetime keeps the cookie on the device longer.

turns.threat: A tester shows that a script on the page can read the session cookie with document.cookie.
turns.constraint: Only the server needs to read the session cookie.

reasons.text: SameSite=Strict also hides the cookie from scripts on the page.
HttpOnly stops JavaScript from reading the cookie, so a bad script cannot steal it.
A shorter lifetime stops scripts from reading the cookie.

moves.counterattack: Scripts cannot read the cookie now, but your own front-end code cannot read it either.
The cookie ends sooner, so a stolen copy works for less time.
Cross-site requests stop carrying the cookie, but the script on your page still reads it.
You start a new session, but scripts can read the new cookie too.

turns.modelAnswer: Set HttpOnly on the session cookie. JavaScript then cannot read it, so a bad script cannot steal it. Only the server uses it. The cost: your front-end code cannot read it either.
keyPoints: HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript.
Session cookies should be HttpOnly.
Front-end code also loses access to the cookie.

scenarios.name: The partner widget
scenarios.problem: Your chat widget runs inside partner sites. Users sign in to the widget there.

turns.threat: The widget's session cookie has no SameSite attribute. Inside partner sites, users are signed out.
turns.constraint: A cookie with no SameSite attribute is treated as Lax by default.

reasons.text: SameSite=None sends the cookie with cross-site requests.
A longer cookie lifetime keeps users signed in on the partner sites.
A cookie with no SameSite attribute goes with requests from any site.

moves.counterattack: The cookie lives longer, but the browser still holds it back inside partner sites.
SameSite=None keeps users signed in, but the cookie loses its cross-site protection.
You check that Set-Cookie arrives, but the browser still holds the cookie back.
You build a new session system, but it still uses a cookie with the same rules.

turns.modelAnswer: Some browsers treat a cookie with no SameSite as Lax. Lax does not go with requests from embedded content on other sites. Set SameSite=None with Secure. The cost: the cookie loses its cross-site protection.
keyPoints: No SameSite can mean Lax in some browsers.
SameSite=None sends the cookie on cross-site requests.
SameSite=None gives up some protection against cross-site attacks.

turns.threat: On the test site, which uses plain http, the browser rejects the new cookie.
turns.constraint: The partner sites use HTTPS, but your test site uses plain http.

reasons.text: Lax works like None inside a frame.
A plain http site can set a Secure cookie for its own test users.
SameSite=None needs Secure, and an http site cannot set a Secure cookie.

moves.counterattack: You switch back to Lax, so users are signed out inside partner sites again.
You send the Set-Cookie header again, but it still cannot work on plain http.
The test site moves to HTTPS, so the Secure cookie works, but the test setup grows.

turns.modelAnswer: SameSite=None needs the Secure attribute. A Secure cookie goes only over HTTPS, and an http site cannot set it. Run the test site on HTTPS. The cost: the test setup gets bigger.
keyPoints: SameSite=None needs Secure.
Secure cookies travel only over HTTPS.
A plain http site cannot set a Secure cookie.

turns.threat: Partner sites ask for the user's whole profile inside one large widget cookie.
turns.constraint: Cookies go with every request, and many users are on slow mobile data.

reasons.text: Many small cookies cost less than one big one.
Keep the profile on the server, and link it with one cookie.
A longer lifetime makes a large cookie cheaper, because it is sent less.

moves.counterattack: The requests now share one session, but the server must keep the session state.
You split the profile over many Set-Cookie headers, but each cookie still goes with every request.
The profile cookie lasts longer, so more old data stays in every browser.
You tighten SameSite, so users are signed out inside partner sites, and the cookie is still large.

turns.modelAnswer: HTTP is stateless, but not sessionless. Cookies let requests share the same state, like one session, so keep the profile on the server. The cost: the server keeps the session.
keyPoints: HTTP itself is stateless.
Cookies let requests share one session.
The server keeps the session state.

scenarios.name: The busy night

source.title: Google SRE book: Load balancing at the frontend

scenarios.problem: A big launch brings many more users tonight than one machine can serve.

turns.threat: Tonight one server must answer every visitor. It cannot handle that load.
turns.constraint: A balancer can forward each request to one of several machines behind one address.

reasons.text: A forward proxy in front of the shop also spreads the load over servers.
A reverse proxy shares the load across several servers.
A friendly 503 page is enough, because the visitors will come back later.

moves.counterattack: A forward proxy works for clients, so your one server still gets every request.
You plan more servers behind one address, but nothing shares the requests between them yet.
You prepare a 503 page, but many visitors see it instead of the shop.
A reverse proxy shares the requests over three servers, but you pay for three servers.

turns.modelAnswer: Put a reverse proxy in front of several web servers. It sends each request to one of them, so they share the load. The cost: you run and pay for more servers.
keyPoints: A reverse proxy sits in front of the servers.
It shares the load across several servers.
More servers cost more to run.

turns.threat: The new servers have a new IP address, but some visitors still reach the old server.
turns.constraint: Resolvers keep the old DNS answer, and nobody can flush their caches.

reasons.text: DNS answers are cached for a while, so some visitors still get the old address.
A DNS change reaches every computer within a few seconds.
A new subdomain moves visitors faster than waiting for the DNS change.

moves.counterattack: You add a new subdomain, but visitors still type the old name.
You keep the old server running until old DNS answers expire, so you pay for both.
You add another new server, but visitors with the old address never reach it.
A forward proxy helps clients, so the old address still sends visitors to the old server.

turns.modelAnswer: Computers and DNS servers keep a domain's data for some time. Then it expires, and they fetch the new IP address. Keep the old server answering until then. The cost: you run both servers for a while.
keyPoints: DNS answers are kept for some time.
Old copies expire and are refreshed later.
Run the old server until the change has spread.

turns.threat: At the peak, all servers are full. New visitors wait and then see a timeout.
turns.constraint: The system is under pressure, and no new machines can join before the peak ends.

reasons.text: A redirect to a waiting page costs the busy servers almost nothing.
Use a 4xx code for too many visitors.
503 says the server is overloaded for now.

moves.counterattack: Visitors see a friendly 503 page with a retry time, but some of them leave.
You answer with a 4xx code, so visitors think they did something wrong.
You redirect visitors to a waiting page, so each one makes another request to busy servers.
A forward proxy works for clients, so the visitors still wait.

turns.modelAnswer: Answer with 503 Service Unavailable when the servers are overloaded. Send a friendly page with it, and a Retry-After header if you can. The cost: some visitors leave.
keyPoints: 503 means the server is overloaded or down for now.
Send a friendly page with the 503.
Retry-After says when to try again.

scenarios.name: The office network
scenarios.problem: Your team of 40 works in one office. The internet line is slow, and staff also work on trains.

turns.threat: Every laptop downloads the same large web pages and files again and again.
turns.constraint: HTTP/1.1 has cache control, and all 40 laptops share one slow line.

reasons.text: A reverse proxy at the office also saves bandwidth for the laptops.
HTTP/2 stops the same file from crossing the slow line twice.
A forward proxy keeps copies for a group of clients.

moves.counterattack: A reverse proxy protects servers, so the laptops still download everything.
The office proxy stores and forwards pages, but it is one more machine to run.
Requests share one connection now, but the same files still cross the line many times.
Lookups come from the cache, but the same large files still cross the line.

turns.modelAnswer: A forward proxy works for a group of clients. It stores and forwards pages, so the group uses less bandwidth. The cost: one more machine to run.
keyPoints: A forward proxy acts for the clients.
It stores and forwards pages for the group.
The proxy is one more machine to run.

turns.threat: A new app on the laptops sends Connection: close, so each request needs a new TCP handshake.
turns.constraint: The app sends many small requests to the same server.

reasons.text: HTTP/1.1 reuses a connection unless told to close it, so one handshake serves many requests.
A faster DNS lookup also removes the TCP handshake before each request.
A reverse proxy keeps the laptops' connections open for them.

moves.counterattack: Lookups come from the cache, but each request still waits for a new handshake.
A reverse proxy stands in front of servers, so the laptops still open new connections.
The app reuses open connections now, but idle connections still use server resources.

turns.modelAnswer: In HTTP/1.1, connections are persistent by default. Connection: close ends the connection after each response. Remove it, so requests reuse one connection. The cost: idle connections still use resources.
keyPoints: HTTP/1.1 keeps connections open by default.
Connection: close forces a new handshake each time.
Idle open connections still use resources.

turns.threat: Staff on the train use the app on a weak phone network. One lost packet stops every image.
turns.constraint: The servers and the app can both be updated to HTTP/3.

reasons.text: HTTP/2 already keeps one lost packet from blocking the other streams.
In QUIC, a lost packet blocks only its own stream.
An open connection is safe from packet loss.

moves.counterattack: HTTP/2 sends requests in parallel, but one lost TCP packet still blocks all streams.
The connection stays open, but a lost packet still blocks the images.
The office proxy cannot help staff on the train.
With HTTP/3 a lost packet blocks only its own stream, but your servers must support HTTP/3.

turns.modelAnswer: HTTP/2 runs over one TCP connection, so a lost packet can block all streams. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. A lost packet then blocks only its own stream. The cost: your servers must support HTTP/3.
keyPoints: In HTTP/2, a lost TCP packet can block all streams.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
In QUIC, a lost packet blocks only its stream.

scenarios.name: Public Wi-Fi
scenarios.problem: Many customers shop on cafe and airport Wi-Fi. Someone on the same network may watch the traffic.

turns.threat: The sign-in page still works over plain http. An attacker on the Wi-Fi can read passwords.
turns.constraint: Anyone on the same Wi-Fi can read unencrypted traffic.

reasons.text: After the TLS handshake, headers and bodies are encrypted.
An HSTS header sent over plain http protects the sign-in form at once.
A Secure cookie also protects the password that the form sends.

moves.counterattack: Browsers ignore HSTS sent over plain http, so nothing changes.
Secure keeps the cookie off plain http, but the password still travels in plain text.
Every header and body now travel encrypted, but each new connection starts with a handshake.
You redirect to another http page, so the password is still in plain text.

turns.modelAnswer: Serve the sign-in page over HTTPS. The TLS handshake agrees on a secret key, and then every header and body is encrypted. The cost: each new connection begins with a handshake.
keyPoints: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.
After the handshake, headers and bodies are encrypted.
Each new TLS connection starts with a handshake.

turns.threat: Customers who type http://shop.example.com reach the plain site first. An attacker can stop the switch to HTTPS.
turns.constraint: Customers come back to the shop many times a month.

reasons.text: A 301 to HTTPS also protects the first plain request, if it is fast.
A new certificate stops an attacker from reading the plain http page.
HSTS makes later visits go straight to HTTPS, even when someone types http.

moves.counterattack: Browsers now go straight to HTTPS until max-age ends, but the very first visit is still open.
The 301 to HTTPS works, but an attacker can still catch that first plain request.
You renew the certificate, but the first plain http request is still open.
Browsers upgrade images, but the page request itself is still plain http.

turns.modelAnswer: A 301 to HTTPS alone leaves the first plain request open. Also send Strict-Transport-Security over HTTPS with a long max-age. Later visits then use HTTPS directly. The cost: the first visit can still be attacked.
keyPoints: A 301 alone leaves the first request open.
HSTS makes the browser use HTTPS directly.
HSTS works only after one HTTPS visit.

turns.threat: A security review says the very first visit of a new customer is still open to attack.
turns.constraint: Every subdomain of the shop already serves HTTPS.

reasons.text: A longer max-age also protects a customer's very first visit.
A preloaded domain uses HTTPS even on the first visit.
TLS 1.3 removes the first-visit risk.

moves.counterattack: TLS 1.3 is current, but the first plain http request is still open.
A longer max-age helps later visits, but the first visit is still open.
Your domain joins the preload list, but every subdomain must now work over HTTPS.

turns.modelAnswer: Join the HSTS preload list. Browsers then use HTTPS for your domain even on the first visit. The header needs a max-age of at least one year, includeSubDomains and preload. The cost: every subdomain must serve HTTPS.
keyPoints: Preloading protects the very first visit.
Preload needs a one-year max-age, includeSubDomains and preload.
Every subdomain must then work over HTTPS.

scenarios.name: The certificate warning
scenarios.problem: After a server move, some customers see a certificate warning. A few of them click through it.

turns.threat: The new server's certificate is for old.example.com, not for shop.example.com.
turns.constraint: The DNS name points to the right server, and TLS 1.3 is on.

reasons.text: Turning on a newer TLS version fixes the name check on the certificate.
The browser only checks that a known CA signed the certificate.
The certificate must name the site the browser asked for.

moves.counterattack: You turn on TLS 1.3, but the name on the certificate is still wrong.
You trace where the server proves its identity, but the name is still wrong.
The name points to the right IP address, but the certificate still names another site.
The new certificate names shop.example.com, but someone must keep it up to date.

turns.modelAnswer: A website certificate names the site it is for, and a CA signs it. The browser checks the name and the chain back to a root. Get a certificate for shop.example.com. The cost: someone must manage it.
keyPoints: The certificate must name the site.
The browser checks the chain back to a root certificate.
Someone must manage the certificate from now on.

turns.threat: Some customers still click through certificate warnings. An attacker could use a fake certificate the same way.
turns.constraint: An attacker in the middle could use a fake certificate on customers who click through.

reasons.text: For an HSTS host, the browser blocks click-through on certificate errors.
A correct certificate stops users from clicking through.
Users stop at the warning when the site matters to them.

moves.counterattack: The right certificate is in place, but users can still click through a future warning.
Browsers stop click-through on certificate errors, but a broken certificate now stops every visitor.
Scripts over http are blocked, but users still click through the warning.

turns.modelAnswer: Send the HSTS header. For an HSTS host, the browser does not let users click through certificate errors. The cost: a broken certificate now stops every visitor.
keyPoints: HSTS blocks click-through on certificate errors.
Users can no longer accept a fake certificate.
A broken certificate now stops every visitor.

turns.threat: A scan shows the server still allows TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.
turns.constraint: Every client the shop supports can use TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3.

reasons.text: A new certificate turns off old TLS.
TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 should no longer be used.
The HSTS preload list also stops browsers from using old TLS versions.

moves.counterattack: You read the handshake steps, but the old versions are still allowed.
Only TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are allowed now, so clients that know only old versions cannot connect.
You get a new certificate, but the old TLS versions are still on.
Preloading forces HTTPS, but the old TLS versions are still allowed.

turns.modelAnswer: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 should no longer be used. TLS 1.3 is the current version, and some sites still use 1.2. Turn off the old versions in the server config. The cost: clients that know only the old versions cannot connect.
keyPoints: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 should no longer be used.
TLS 1.3 is current, and 1.2 is still in use.
The server config decides the allowed versions.

scenarios.name: The broken menu
scenarios.problem: The shop moved to HTTPS. Now the menu does not work, and the browser console shows warnings.

turns.threat: The HTTPS page loads its menu script from http://cdn.example.com/menu.js.
turns.constraint: The developer console says the menu script request was blocked.

reasons.text: The browser upgrades every http request on the page to https by itself.
Browsers block a script over http on an HTTPS page.
A redirect from http to https on the CDN makes the script load.

moves.counterattack: You wait for the browser to upgrade it, but scripts are blocked, not upgraded.
The page itself is encrypted, but the browser still blocks the http script.

moves.counterattack: You still decide alone what is big, so surprises continue.

moves.label: Let us meet every morning for half an hour.
moves.counterattack: Your manager knows more, but both of you lose time every day.

moves.label: I will send a short weekly update with my focus and my risks.
moves.counterattack: It takes you some time each week, but your manager sees problems early.
