turns.modelAnswer: Offer a short weekly update, like an email or a Slack thread. Share your focus and your risks. The cost: you spend some time each week on it.
keyPoints: Send a short weekly update.
Share your focus and your risks.
Use writing, not more meetings.

turns.threat: Should the team change its priorities to catch up?
turns.constraint: You have the numbers on where the two weeks went.

reasons.text: You know the work best, so it is fine to move people and tell them after.
Data and a question about priorities beat an opinion.
A clear opinion saves your manager time, so give it without the numbers.

moves.label: Here are the numbers on the delay. How do our priorities fit with yours?
moves.counterattack: The talk takes longer, but you and your manager agree on a plan.

moves.label: I feel we should drop the blog work and move faster.
moves.counterattack: Your manager hears an opinion with nothing to check.

moves.label: I already moved two people from the blog to the HTTPS work.
moves.counterattack: Your manager is surprised a second time in one meeting.

turns.modelAnswer: Bring the numbers, not only an opinion. Then ask how the team's priorities fit with your manager's. The cost: the decision takes one more talk.
keyPoints: Bring data, not only an opinion.
Ask how your priorities fit your manager's.
Do not decide alone and surprise again.

scenarios.name: Five minutes with the CTO

source.title: StaffEng: Getting in the room, presenting to executives

scenarios.problem: You present a plan to move every company site to HTTPS. The CTO has a short slot for it.

turns.threat: So, what do you need from me?
turns.constraint: The meeting has only a few minutes for your topic.

reasons.text: The CTO needs the history first, or the proposal will make no sense.
Give the summary first, then the details.
Three options with no proposal let the CTO choose freely.

moves.label: Let me first explain how our setup grew over the years.
moves.counterattack: The time runs out before you reach your point.

moves.label: We should move every site to HTTPS this quarter. I need your yes on the plan today.
moves.counterattack: The CTO asks hard questions, but can decide now.

moves.label: There are three ways to do it. Which one do you like?
moves.counterattack: The CTO must do your thinking, and the room cannot align.

turns.modelAnswer: Start with the summarizing idea: the proposal and the decision you need. A short SCQA opening works well. The cost: you must cut most of your details.
keyPoints: Give the answer first.
Bring a proposal, not only a question.
Say what you need from the CTO.

turns.threat: I think this plan is too slow.
turns.constraint: The comment is new to you, and you need time to judge it.

reasons.text: A firm defence in the room shows the CTO that the plan is solid.
Agree at once to keep the CTO happy.
Gather the feedback now, and judge it later.

moves.label: The plan is right, and here is why that view is wrong.
moves.counterattack: The CTO stops giving you honest comments.

moves.label: OK, we will do it in half the time.
moves.counterattack: You avoid a fight, but you promise a date you never checked.

moves.label: Thank you. What would make it fast enough for you?
moves.counterattack: You do not win the point now, but you learn what the CTO needs.

turns.modelAnswer: Never fight feedback. Ask questions to learn what the CTO needs. Decide later, with more time, whether you agree. The cost: you do not win the point in the room.
keyPoints: Never fight feedback.
Ask what the CTO needs.
Decide later whether you agree.

turns.threat: What is the biggest risk in this plan?
turns.constraint: One old partner system may break, and nobody has tested it yet.

reasons.text: Name the problem and your answer to it, even when the answer is not finished.
Naming an untested risk in the room may get the whole plan rejected.
Wait until you have tested it, so you bring facts and not fears.

moves.label: There are no big risks in this plan.
moves.counterattack: The CTO finds the risk later and trusts you less.

moves.label: One old partner system may break. We test it first and keep a way back.
moves.counterattack: The plan looks less perfect, but the CTO trusts it more.

moves.label: I will come back to you on the risks next week.
moves.counterattack: The decision waits a week.

turns.modelAnswer: Do not evade problems. Name the biggest risk and your answer to it. The cost: the plan looks less perfect in the room.
keyPoints: Do not hide the problem.
Name the biggest risk.
Give your answer to the risk.

scenarios.name: The growing wish list

source.title: Shape Up: Decide when to stop

scenarios.problem: A client's new checkout must launch at the end of a fixed six-week project. The client keeps adding wishes.

turns.threat: Can you also add saved cards before launch?
turns.constraint: The launch date is fixed, and the must-haves fill the six weeks.

reasons.text: A good team can usually fit one more small feature into six weeks.
Moving the date is the honest way to add scope for the client.
With a fixed date and a full plan, a new wish goes on the nice-to-have list.

moves.label: Yes, the team will work extra hours to fit it in.
moves.counterattack: Saved cards may arrive, but tired people make more mistakes.

moves.label: Yes, if we move the launch by two weeks.
moves.counterattack: The fixed date is gone, and the next wish moves it again.

moves.label: Saved cards go on the nice-to-have list. We add them if time is left.
moves.counterattack: The client is a little unhappy, but the launch date holds.

turns.modelAnswer: Keep the date and vary the scope. Put saved cards on the nice-to-have list, and do them only if time is left. The cost: the client may not get them in this launch.
keyPoints: The date is fixed, and the scope can change.
A new wish is a nice-to-have.
Nice-to-haves are cut if there is no time.

turns.threat: The new checkout is not perfect. Should we wait?
turns.constraint: Today, shoppers must phone the shop to place a large order.

reasons.text: Compare to what shoppers have today, not to the ideal.
A launch with known gaps will hurt the client's name more than a delay.
A full list of every gap is the most honest answer you can give.

moves.label: It is not perfect, but it is much better than phoning in an order today.
moves.counterattack: The client still sees the gaps, but agrees to launch.

moves.label: Yes, we wait until every detail is perfect.
moves.counterattack: The launch slips again and again.

moves.label: Here is a list of every gap we know about.
moves.counterattack: The client sees only problems and loses confidence.

turns.modelAnswer: Compare down to the baseline, the shoppers' life today, not up to the ideal. The new checkout is better than phoning in an order. The cost: you launch with known gaps.
keyPoints: Compare to the baseline, not the ideal.
Better than today is a reason to ship.
You launch with some known gaps.

turns.threat: The team needs two more weeks. Can we just extend the project?
turns.constraint: All the must-haves are done. Only nice-to-haves are left.

reasons.text: Two more weeks is a small price for a checkout with every wish in it.
When the must-haves are done, the scope is done, so cut the nice-to-haves.
A project that runs past its time box should be stopped, not shipped.

moves.label: Yes, two more weeks makes the checkout complete.
moves.counterattack: The checkout gets nicer, but the next project starts late.

moves.label: The must-haves are done, so we launch now and cut the rest.
moves.counterattack: A few wishes wait, but the checkout ships on time.

moves.label: No, we stop the project here.
moves.counterattack: The client loses a checkout that was ready to ship.

turns.modelAnswer: The must-haves are done, so the scope is done. Cut the nice-to-haves and launch. The cost: a few wishes wait for a later project.
keyPoints: The must-haves are done.
Cut the nice-to-haves.
Ship on the fixed date.

scenarios.name: The VP on the phone
scenarios.problem: The shop's sign-in is down. Your manager, a VP, calls you in the middle of the incident.

turns.threat: What is happening? Should I join the call?
turns.constraint: Three teams are on the call, and nobody owns the updates yet.

reasons.text: A VP on the call helps the team decide faster and remove blockers.
Leaders need every detail, or they cannot decide well.
One lead and short scheduled updates keep leaders informed.

moves.label: Yes, join the call and hear everything.
moves.counterattack: One more voice joins, and the call gets slower.

moves.label: Let me walk you through every log line we have seen so far.
moves.counterattack: Your manager is informed, but you stop fixing the problem.

moves.label: One person now leads the incident. I will email you short status updates on a schedule.
moves.counterattack: Your manager waits for news, but the team can work.

turns.modelAnswer: Name one incident lead, and give one person the job of updates. Send short status emails to a fixed list. The cost: your manager does not hear every detail.
keyPoints: One person leads the incident.
One person sends regular updates.
Keep updates high-level for leaders.

turns.threat: An engineer wants to try his own fix right now. Can he?
turns.constraint: Nobody else on the call knows what he wants to change.

reasons.text: A senior engineer should fix things at once, because every minute counts.
Changes go through the incident lead, so nobody is surprised.
No changes at all is the safest rule until the outage ends.

moves.label: Yes, every minute counts.
moves.counterattack: His change surprises the others and makes the outage worse.

moves.label: Yes, but only after he tells the incident lead what he will change.
moves.counterattack: The fix starts a few minutes later, but nobody is surprised.

moves.label: No, nobody changes anything until the outage is over.
moves.counterattack: Nothing gets worse, but nothing gets fixed either.

turns.modelAnswer: Every change goes through the incident lead. A change made alone, even with good intentions, can make a bad situation worse. The cost: the fix starts a few minutes later.
keyPoints: Do not let people fix things alone.
Changes go through the incident lead.
Everyone must know what is changing.

turns.threat: It was small in the end. Was it worth calling an incident?
turns.constraint: The fix took ten minutes once the right person looked at it.

reasons.text: It is better to declare early, find a simple fix and close the incident.
Declare an incident only once you know the cause.
An incident is for problems that customers can see, not for small ones.

moves.label: Yes. Declaring it early cost little, and we closed it fast.
moves.counterattack: Some calls will turn out small, but none grow out of control.

moves.label: No, next time we wait until we are sure it is big.
moves.counterattack: The next big outage starts with nobody in charge.

moves.label: Only when customers can see the problem.
moves.counterattack: That is one good rule, but hidden problems now grow alone.

turns.modelAnswer: Yes. It is better to declare an incident early, find a simple fix and close it. Set clear conditions for declaring one. The cost: some incidents turn out small.
keyPoints: Declare incidents early.
Close them fast when the fix is simple.
Set clear conditions for declaring one.

scenarios.name: The open CORS door

source.title: PortSwigger Research: Exploiting CORS misconfigurations for Bitcoins and bounties

scenarios.problem: A partner site cannot call your API. An AI agent changed the CORS headers to make it work.

turns.threat: The API now copies any Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin, with credentials.
turns.constraint: Replies carry each signed-in user's private API key.

reasons.text: With credentials on, the browser checks the origin for the server.
The browser blocks other sites anyway, because the API needs a cookie.
Copying any origin with credentials lets any site read private data.

moves.counterattack: Any site can now read a signed-in user's private API key.
A test may catch it, but the open door ships tonight if nobody looks.
The partner waits one more day, but no other site can read user data.

turns.modelAnswer: Block it. Copying the Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin, with credentials, trusts every site. Any site can then read a signed-in user's data. The cost: the partner waits.
keyPoints: Copying the Origin header trusts every site.
With credentials, other sites can read private data.
Block the change before the release.

turns.threat: The agent now trusts every origin that ends in example.com.
turns.constraint: No test sends a request from an origin like evilexample.com.

reasons.text: An end-of-name check also trusts lookalike names that an attacker can register.
Every name that ends in example.com belongs to the company.
A test would only repeat what the new check already says.

moves.counterattack: You stop it again, but the agent does not learn which case is wrong.
The test fails for evilexample.com, and the agent must fix the check.
A site named evilexample.com can now read user data.

turns.modelAnswer: Ask for a test with an origin like evilexample.com. A check on the end of the name trusts names that an attacker can register. The test shows the bug, so the agent can fix it. The cost: one more round.
keyPoints: An end-of-name check is not safe.
Ask for a test with a lookalike origin.
A failing test shows the agent what to fix.

turns.threat: The agent now allows only one exact origin from a fixed list, and adds Vary: Origin.
turns.constraint: A test shows that an unknown origin gets no CORS headers.

reasons.text: Changes to CORS headers are risky, so block them until a security review.
An exact list, with a test for unknown origins, is evidence.
Ask for one more test, to be safe, even if the right one already exists.

moves.counterattack: The test you want is already there, so the partner waits for nothing.
You block a safe change, and the partner still cannot call the API.
The partner site works, and you must keep the list up to date.

turns.modelAnswer: Approve it. The API trusts one exact origin from a fixed list, and sends Vary: Origin. A test proves an unknown origin gets nothing. The cost: someone must keep the list up to date.
keyPoints: Trust exact origins from a fixed list.
Send Vary: Origin with a dynamic header.
Approve when a test is the evidence.

scenarios.name: The cached account page

source.title: Game Informer: Valve provides more information on Steam's troubled Christmas

scenarios.problem: The store is under heavy load. An AI agent added caching rules to make pages faster.

turns.threat: The account page, which shows a billing address, is now cached for every user.
turns.constraint: A shared web cache sits in front of the store.

reasons.text: A shared cache can serve one user's page to another.
A page behind sign-in is never kept by a shared cache.
A short max-age makes a public cache safe for private pages.

moves.counterattack: The account page stays slower, but no user sees another user's page.
Users start to see account pages that were made for other users.
A test may show it, but the risk is clear from the diff.

turns.modelAnswer: Block it. A shared cache that stores pages for signed-in users can serve one user's page to another. On Steam, this showed personal data to other users. The cost: the account page stays slower.
keyPoints: Pages for signed-in users must not be shared.
A shared cache can show one user's page to another.
Block it before it ships.

turns.threat: The diff also caches the public store pages, which take most of the attack traffic.
turns.constraint: The store is under a DoS attack, and caching takes load off its servers.

reasons.text: A diff should be approved or blocked as a whole, not cut into parts.
Keep the public caching, and drop the signed-in part.
Caching is safe once most pages are public, so the rest can stay.

moves.counterattack: The store pages get faster, and the account pages leak too.
Only the public page caching ships, and the account change waits.
Nothing leaks, but the store servers carry the whole attack.

turns.modelAnswer: Narrow it. Caching public pages takes load off the servers during the attack. Remove the part that caches pages for signed-in users. The cost: the agent must split its work.
keyPoints: Split the safe part from the risky part.
Caching public pages takes load off the servers.
Pages for signed-in users must not be cached.

turns.threat: The agent removes the account page rule and says the old cached copies will expire soon.
turns.constraint: Pages made for other users are still on the cache's edge servers right now.

reasons.text: Fixing the rule also removes the copies that are already cached.
The old copies expire soon, so the risk is over in a few minutes.
Old copies keep leaking to other users until the cached data is purged.

moves.counterattack: Users keep seeing other users' pages until the old copies expire.
The rule change ships, but nothing removes the old copies.
The store stays closed longer, but no old copy reaches another user.

turns.modelAnswer: Block it until the cached pages are purged. A new rule does not remove the copies already on the edge servers. Valve kept the store down until the cached data was purged. The cost: the store stays down longer.
keyPoints: A new rule does not remove old copies.
Purge the cached data on the edge servers.
Keep the store down until the purge is done.

scenarios.name: The double charge

source.title: Stripe: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency

scenarios.problem: Some card charges fail with network errors. An AI agent added retries to the charge call.

turns.threat: The client may now send the same charge up to three times.
turns.constraint: The charge call sends no Idempotency-Key header.

reasons.text: A request that failed with a network error never reached the server.
After a network error, a retry can charge twice.
Three tries rarely charge twice.

moves.counterattack: A test may find it later, but the diff already shows the risk.
The failed charges stay failed for now, but no customer pays twice.
Some customers are charged two or three times.

turns.modelAnswer: Block it. After a network error, the client cannot know if the charge happened. A blind retry can charge the customer twice. The cost: failed charges stay failed until there is a safe fix.
keyPoints: A network error does not mean the charge failed.
A blind retry can charge twice.
Block until the retry is safe.

turns.threat: The agent now sends one Idempotency-Key per order, the same on every retry, but retries at once.
turns.constraint: After an outage, thousands of clients retry at the same moment.

reasons.text: Retries with no wait hit the API together, so the outage can get longer.
A retry should go out at once, so the customer waits less.
The idempotency key also spreads the retries out over time.

moves.counterattack: The clients hit the API all at once, and the outage gets longer.
The fix waits one more round, but the retries will not hit the API together.
You keep the key and drop the retries, so failed charges stay failed.

turns.modelAnswer: Block it and ask for exponential backoff with random jitter. The key is right, but retries with no wait hit the API together. This is a thundering herd. The cost: one more round for the agent.
keyPoints: The same key on every retry is right.
Retries with no wait cause a thundering herd.
Ask for exponential backoff with jitter.

turns.threat: The agent adds exponential backoff with random jitter between retries.
turns.constraint: Each retry sends the same Idempotency-Key, and the waits grow with random jitter.

reasons.text: The same key plus backoff with jitter make retries safe.
Waiting between retries makes customers wait, so it should be short and fixed.
Random waits make a payment system harder to predict and less safe.

moves.counterattack: You cut part of a safe change, and the agent has to redo it.
Retries now help, but the code is longer to read.
You block a safe fix, and charges keep failing.

turns.modelAnswer: Approve it. The same idempotency key lets the server spot a retry, so there is no double charge. Backoff with jitter stops clients from retrying at the same moment. The cost: more code to read.
keyPoints: The same key lets the server spot a retry.
Backoff with jitter spreads retries out.
Approve, and own the verdict.

scenarios.name: The open redirect

source.title: OWASP: Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards Cheat Sheet

scenarios.problem: Users want to return to their last page after sign-in. An AI agent added a next parameter.

turns.threat: The sign-in page now redirects to any URL in the next parameter.
turns.constraint: The next value can be any full URL, and nothing checks it.

reasons.text: A link with the shop's real name can lead users to a fake site.
Users read the address bar after a redirect.
A redirect only changes the page, so it cannot leak any data.

moves.counterattack: Users still land on their account page for now, but no link can send them away.
A test may show it, but the risk is clear from the diff.
A phishing link now shows the shop's own name and lands on a fake site.

turns.modelAnswer: Block it. The redirect takes its target from user input. A phishing link then starts on the real shop, so users trust it. The cost: users do not return to their last page yet.
keyPoints: The target comes from user input.
The link shows the trusted shop name.
Block it until the target is checked.

turns.threat: The agent now accepts any full URL in next whose host is on a list of partner sites.
turns.constraint: After sign-in, users only ever return to pages of the shop itself.

reasons.text: A list of partner hosts is as safe as local paths.
Checking the host makes any redirect safe.
Local return URLs need only a helper that rejects other hosts.

moves.counterattack: The list works, but every partner on it is now a place to send users.
You block it, and the agent does not learn which part is wrong.
Next now takes only local paths, and partner pages need another way.

turns.modelAnswer: Narrow it. Users only return to shop pages, so accept only local return URLs. Use the framework helper that rejects non-local destinations. The cost: partner pages need another way.
keyPoints: Users only return to the shop.
Accept only local return URLs.
Use the framework helper for local URLs.

turns.threat: The agent now uses the framework helper that rejects non-local return URLs.
turns.constraint: A test shows that a next value with another site's URL goes to the account page.

reasons.text: A redirect that uses user input should be blocked in every case.
A local-only helper, with a test for outside URLs, is evidence.
A short diff needs no review once the tests pass.

moves.counterattack: Users return to their last page, and you own the decision.
You block a safe change, and users still lose their page.
The test you want is already there, so the change waits for nothing.

turns.modelAnswer: Approve it. The framework helper rejects non-local targets, and a test proves an outside URL goes nowhere. The cost: you own this decision now.
keyPoints: Use a helper that rejects non-local URLs.
A test is the evidence.
Approve and own the verdict.

intro.title: How a good API is shaped
screens: An API is built from resources: named things, like the books of a publisher. A collection holds resources of the same type.
A small number of standard methods do most of the work. A custom method is only for the cases where the standard methods do not fit.
Example: a client asks for book 1, then for book 2. These two calls are independent of each other. The client and the server each have a clear role.
The API is not a copy of your database. An API that matches the database schema ties the outside to the inside.
intro.diagram:
flowchart TD
  A[Resource and URL] --> B[Auth with an access token]
  B --> C[Rate limit and 429]
  C --> D[Paging and conditional requests]
  D --> E[Status code and problem details]
  E --> F[Idempotency key and safe retry]
  F --> G[Long-running operation]
  G --> H[OpenAPI description]
  H --> I[Versioning and breaking changes]

screens.text: Picture a library API. It has publishers, and each publisher has books. Publishers and books are things. In API words, things are called resources.
AIP-121 says an API is built from individually named resources, the nouns. The relationships and hierarchy between them matter too. Resources form a hierarchy of simple resources and collections.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Publisher] --> B[Books collection]
  B --> C[One book]

screens.text: A small set of standard methods, the verbs, gives the meaning of most operations. They are Get, List, Create, Update and Delete. AIP-121 also calls an API identical to the database schema an anti-pattern. It couples the API tightly to the system below.

catch.question: In resource-oriented design, what are the main building blocks of an API?
choices: Actions, with one endpoint for each task
Named resources, the nouns, and the links between them
The database tables, with one endpoint for each table
The app screens, with one endpoint for each screen
catch.explanation: AIP-121 says the building blocks are named resources, the nouns, with their relationships and hierarchy.

card.text: Resource-oriented design is a way to design APIs. The building blocks are named resources, the nouns, and the relationships between them. A small set of standard methods, the verbs, covers most operations. Custom methods are for cases the standard methods do not fit. Each request is independent of the others: the protocol is stateless. The API should not copy the database schema. AIP-121 calls an API identical to the database schema an anti-pattern.
card.example: A publisher has the collection of books that it publishes. A client reads one book with Get and changes it with Update. It lists the books with List.

review.question: Why should an API not copy the database schema?
review.answer: It ties the API surface to the system below it. AIP-121 calls this an anti-pattern.

workedExample.problem: Your team plans the endpoints /getBookById, /saveNewBook and /removeBookNow for a library API.
steps: List the nouns first: publishers and books.
Find the relationship: a publisher has a collection of books.
Map each action to a standard method: Get, Create and Delete.
workedExample.answer: Design books as a resource under publishers, and use the standard methods instead of one endpoint per action.

tradeOff.situation: Your database has 40 tables. A developer wants one API endpoint for each table, because it is quick to build.
options: Expose one endpoint for each table, exactly as it is
Design resources and relationships for the clients, and map them to the tables
Expose the tables now, and add client-friendly resources in version 2

reasons.text: Copying the database schema is an anti-pattern, because it couples the API tightly to the system below.
One endpoint for each table is quick to build, and the clients can join the data they need.
Shipping the tables first gives clients something today, and version 2 can hide the tables later.

tradeOff.explanation: AIP-121 says an API should not expect to reflect the database schema, so design resources first. The cost is more design work before you write endpoints.

decisionCards.situation: Your API needs to remember where each client is in a long form. Do you store this application state on the server between calls?
options: Keep the client's application state on the server
Make each request independent, and let the client keep its own state

reasons.text: Server sessions are the usual way to track a form, and a sticky load balancer handles them.
Stateless means the server stores no data, so it cannot save the form answers between calls.
The protocol must be stateless: each request stands on its own, and the client keeps application state.

decisionCards.explanation: AIP-121 says the server persists data, but the client has sole responsibility for application state. So the client code must manage that state itself.

screens.text: A resource name is how a client points to one resource. It follows the URI path form, but it has no leading slash. A resource must also have a name field that holds this name.

AIP-122 says a name usually alternates between collection identifiers and resource IDs. Collection identifiers are plural nouns in camelCase. Resource IDs should not use upper-case letters. Segments are separated by slashes.
Example: publishers/123/books/les-miserables. Here publishers and books are collection identifiers. 123 and les-miserables are resource IDs. Another name is users/vhugo1802.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[publishers collection] --> B[ID 123]
  B --> C[books collection]
  C --> D[ID les-miserables]

catch.question: Which resource name follows Google AIP-122?
catch.explanation: A name alternates between plural collection identifiers and resource IDs. It uses slashes and has no leading slash.

card.text: Each resource has a unique name. Users store this name to refer to the resource. A name follows the URI path schema, but without the leading slash. It usually alternates between collection identifiers and resource IDs. Collection identifiers are plural nouns in camelCase, like publishers or books. Resource IDs should not use upper-case letters. A resource must have a name field that holds its resource name.
card.example: publishers/123/books/les-miserables names one book. publishers and books are collection identifiers. 123 and les-miserables are resource IDs. users/vhugo1802 names one user.

review.question: What do the parts of publishers/123/books/les-miserables alternate between?
review.answer: Collection identifiers, like books, and resource IDs, like les-miserables.

screens.text: Most API work is one of five jobs: read one, read many, add, change and remove. AIP-121 gives each job a standard method: Get, List, Create, Update and Delete.
Every resource must support at least Get. Clients use Get to validate the state of a resource after they change it.
Example: after a successful create, a Get request must return the resource. After a successful delete, a Get must return NOT_FOUND. List is also required, except for singleton resources.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>API: Create book
  Client->>API: Get book
  API-->>Client: The book

catch.question: AIP-121 names one method that every resource must support at minimum, so clients can check a change. Which one?
catch.explanation: A resource must support at least Get. Then clients can check its state after Create, Update or Delete.

card.text: Most operations use five standard methods: Get, List, Create, Update and Delete. Create and Update send the resource and return it. Get returns the resource. List returns the resources. Delete sends and returns no resource. Every resource must support at least Get, so clients can check its state after a change. It must also support List, except a singleton resource. The resource schema must be the same in all methods.
card.example: A client creates a book with Create and gets the book back. Then it calls Get on the same book to check the saved values.

review.question: Which two standard methods must a normal resource support?
review.answer: Get and List. A singleton resource needs only Get.

screens.text: Standard methods do not cover every action. Archiving a book is one case. AIP-136 allows a custom method, but only when standard methods cannot easily express the action. Prefer standard methods, because their meaning is consistent.
A custom method does not add a new HTTP verb. It uses only GET or POST. GET retrieves data. POST is for side effects. The URI puts a colon before the custom verb.
Example: POST /v1/publishers/123/books/456:archive. The method name is a verb and a noun, like ArchiveBook. The name must not contain prepositions.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>API: POST /v1/publishers/123/books/456:archive
  API-->>Client: Result

catch.question: You need an action that archives a book, and no standard method fits. Which call follows AIP-136?
catch.explanation: A custom method uses POST when it changes data. The URI ends with a colon and the custom verb.

card.text: A custom method is for an action that standard methods cannot express well. Prefer standard methods when they fit, because their meaning is consistent. A custom method does not add a new HTTP verb. It uses GET to read data, and POST when it changes data. The URI ends with a colon and the custom verb, like :archive. The name is a verb and a noun, like ArchiveBook, with no prepositions like for or with.
card.example: ArchiveBook is called with POST /v1/publishers/123/books/456:archive. TranslateText is a stateless custom method: POST /v1/projects/my-project:translateText.

review.question: When should you use a custom method instead of a standard method?
review.answer: Only when the action does not fit Get, List, Create, Update or Delete.

screens.text: A status code is the first thing a client reads. The Azure guidelines say to use proper response codes. Then customers can diagnose their own problems and fix them.
Azure gives a table for calls that finish at once. A POST that creates a resource returns 201 Created with the URL of the created resource. A POST action returns 200 OK. GET returns 200 OK.
Example: POST /orders creates an order, so the service returns 201 Created and the order URL. DELETE returns 204 No Content. A call that finishes later returns 202 Accepted.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Service: POST /orders
  Service-->>Client: 201 Created and the order URL

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: HTTP return codes

catch.question: A POST creates a new order, and the service picks its ID. What should the response be, per the Azure guidelines?
choices: 200 OK with the order in the body
201 Created with the URL of the new order
catch.explanation: Azure says a POST that creates a resource returns 201 Created with the URL of the created resource.

card.text: Use the right status code, so customers can find and fix their own problems. The Azure guidelines give a table for calls that finish at once. PUT and PATCH return 200 OK or 201 Created. A POST that creates a resource returns 201 Created with its URL. A POST action returns 200 OK. GET returns 200 OK. DELETE returns 204 No Content, also when the resource does not exist. A call that finishes later returns 202 Accepted.
card.example: DELETE /users/Bob returns 204 No Content with no body. If Bob was already deleted, it returns 204 again, not 404 Not Found.

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: HTTP return codes

review.question: What does an Azure-style API return for a DELETE of a resource that does not exist?
review.answer: 204 No Content, not 404 Not Found.

workedExample.problem: A user asks for an order of another customer. Your API returns 403 Forbidden, so anyone can learn which orders exist.
steps: Azure says to return 403 Forbidden when the user has no access to the resource.
403 is easier to debug, but it says the resource exists.
When that could leak customer secrets, Azure says the response should be 404 Not Found.
workedExample.answer: Return 404 Not Found for orders of other customers, so the API does not show that they exist.

tradeOff.situation: A client calls DELETE on a user that is already deleted. Your team wants to return an error, so the client knows nothing happened.
options: Return 204 No Content with no body
Return 404 Not Found, because the resource does not exist
Return 200 OK with a body that says nothing was deleted

reasons.text: 404 is the usual answer for a missing resource, and clients already handle it well.
A DELETE returns 204 No Content even for a resource that does not exist, not 404.
A body that explains nothing was deleted tells the client more than a status code.

tradeOff.explanation: Azure says DELETE returns 204 No Content even when the resource does not exist. The cost is that the status code alone does not show if the resource existed before.

decisionCards.situation: A POST starts a job that finishes later, like a large report. Which status code does the service return first?
options: 200 OK with a job ID in the body
202 Accepted, and follow the long-running operation guidance

reasons.text: When a PUT, POST or DELETE completes asynchronously, the first answer is 202 Accepted.
A 200 OK with a job ID is enough, since the client can check the job later.
201 Created fits better, because the POST creates a job resource on the server.

decisionCards.explanation: Azure says to return 202 Accepted for a call that completes asynchronously and to follow its guidance on long-running operations. This needs more work than a single answer.

screens.text: 201 Created means the request was fulfilled and created one or more new resources. A client needs to know which resource is the new one. RFC 9110 says where to look.

The primary new resource is identified by the Location header. If there is no Location header, the new resource is the target URI. The response content usually describes the new resource and links to it.
Example: POST /orders returns 201 Created and a Location header with /orders/42. The client keeps /orders/42 to read the order later.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Server: POST /orders
  Server-->>Client: 201 Created and Location /orders/42

catch.question: Where does a 201 Created response say which resource was created?
choices: In the Location header, or else it is the target URI
In the reason phrase of the status line
catch.explanation: The Location header names the main new resource. With no Location header, the new resource is the target URI.

card.text: 201 Created means the request worked and created one or more new resources. The Location header names the main new resource. With no Location header, the new resource is the target URI. The response content usually describes the new resource and links to it. A validator in the response, like an ETag, belongs to the new representation.
card.example: POST /orders returns 201 Created with Location: /orders/42. The client keeps /orders/42 to read the order later.

review.question: Which header of a 201 response names the new resource?
review.answer: The Location header. Without it, the target URI is the new resource.

screens.text: RFC 9110 has client error codes for content that the server will not take. Two are close: 415 and 422. They fail for different reasons.
415 Unsupported Media Type means the server does not support the content format for this method and resource. The cause may be the Content-Type, the Content-Encoding or the data itself.

422 Unprocessable Content means the server understands the content type, and the syntax is correct. But it cannot process the instructions. RFC 9110 gives well-formed XML with semantic errors as an example.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Server: Valid JSON with quantity minus 3
  Server-->>Client: 422 Unprocessable Content

catch.question: A request has valid JSON and a supported Content-Type, but the server cannot process the instructions in it. Which code fits?
catch.explanation: 422 means the server understands the content type and the syntax is correct, but it cannot process the instructions.

card.text: RFC 9110 has three client error codes for content the server will not take. 400 Bad Request is for a client error, like malformed syntax. 415 Unsupported Media Type is for content in a format the server does not support. 422 Unprocessable Content means the content type is understood and the syntax is correct. But the server cannot process the instructions in it.
card.example: A client sends valid JSON with Content-Type: application/json, but the quantity is minus 3. The server answers 422 Unprocessable Content. Broken JSON gets 400 Bad Request.

review.question: What is the difference between 415 and 422?
review.answer: 415: the format is not supported. 422: format and syntax are fine, but the server cannot process the instructions.

screens.text: Two users can change the same resource. The second request may clash with the first change. RFC 9110 has a status code for this.

409 Conflict means the request could not be completed, because it conflicts with the current state of the target resource. Conflicts happen most often with PUT. The new version conflicts with changes from an earlier request.
The user might be able to resolve the conflict and send the request again. So the response should include enough information to find the source of the conflict. Example: two editors change one page.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  EditorA->>Server: PUT page
  EditorB->>Server: PUT page
  Server-->>EditorB: 409 Conflict

catch.question: A PUT would overwrite changes that another user made a moment earlier. Which code does RFC 9110 describe for this?
catch.explanation: 409 means the request conflicts with the current state. RFC 9110 gives a similar PUT example, where a new version conflicts with an earlier change.

card.text: 409 Conflict means the request conflicts with the current state of the target resource. The user might be able to resolve the conflict and send the request again. So the response should give enough information to find the source of the conflict. Conflicts happen most often with PUT. For example, the new version conflicts with changes from an earlier request by someone else.
card.example: Two editors change the same page. The second PUT gets 409 Conflict, and the body shows the other change, so the editor can merge both.

review.question: What should a 409 Conflict response contain?
review.answer: Enough information for the user to find the source of the conflict and resolve it.

screens.text: A status code cannot always give enough information about an error to be helpful. RFC 9457 defines one standard error format for this. It is called problem details.
In JSON, problem details use the media type application/problem+json. The members are type, title, status, detail and instance. Problem details work with any status code. They fit 4xx and 5xx best.

Example: a purchase fails with 403 Forbidden. The Content-Type is application/problem+json. The body has type https://example.com/probs/out-of-credit. The status member must match the real HTTP status code.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Server: Buy item
  Server-->>Client: 403 with application/problem+json

source.title: RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs

catch.question: Which media type does RFC 9457 define for an error body in JSON?
catch.explanation: Problem details in JSON use the media type application/problem+json.

card.text: A status code cannot always say enough about an error. RFC 9457 defines a standard JSON format for error details, called problem details. Its media type is application/problem+json. The members are type, title, status, detail and instance. Problem details work with any status code, but they fit 4xx and 5xx best. The status member must match the real HTTP status code.
card.example: A purchase fails with 403 Forbidden. The body has type https://example.com/probs/out-of-credit and title You do not have enough credit. Its detail is: Your current balance is 30, but that costs 50.

source.title: RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs

review.question: Name the five standard members of a problem details object.
review.answer: type, title, status, detail and instance.

workedExample.problem: Each team in your company returns errors in its own JSON shape. The app needs a different parser for each API.
steps: Pick one standard format for every API: problem details.
Send it with the media type application/problem+json.
Give each error a type URI, a short title and a detail for this case.
workedExample.answer: Use RFC 9457 problem details in every API, so one parser in the app reads every error.

tradeOff.situation: Five teams return errors in their own JSON shapes. One app must read all five APIs, and you pick one format for the company.
options: Let each team keep its own shape, and write each shape in a wiki
Return only status codes, because they are already standard
Use RFC 9457 problem details with application/problem+json in every API

reasons.text: A wiki page for each shape costs far less than changing five APIs that already work in production.
Status codes are already standard, so the app can branch on them without reading a body.
With one standard format, no API has to invent its own. Problem types can still add extension members.

tradeOff.explanation: RFC 9457 gives one standard format, and a problem type can add extension members for extra data. The cost is that each team must change the errors it returns now.

decisionCards.situation: A database error breaks a purchase. What does the problem details response show to the client?
options: A short title and a general detail, without the stack dump
The full stack dump, so support can debug faster

reasons.text: The client already got an error, so a stack dump only adds detail it can ignore.
Implementation details such as a stack dump should stay out of what the HTTP interface shows.
Support needs the stack dump fast, and only our own app reads these responses.

decisionCards.explanation: RFC 9457 warns that leaked details can help attackers or expose user privacy. Support then needs another way to find the cause.

screens.text: An error has text for people and data for programs. A client should not guess from text. It needs one main identifier to tell problems apart.
RFC 9457 says clients must use the type URI as the primary identifier of the problem type. The title is only a short human-readable summary of the problem type.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Error body] --> B[type URI]
  B --> C[App picks the action]

screens.text: If type is missing, its default value is about:blank. Clients should not fetch the type URI automatically. Example: an out-of-credit error has type https://example.com/probs/out-of-credit.

catch.question: What must a client use as the main identifier of a problem?
catch.explanation: Consumers must use the type URI as the primary identifier of the problem type.

card.text: The type member is a URI that identifies the problem type. Clients must use it as the main identifier of the problem. When type is missing, its value is about:blank. That means the problem has no meaning beyond the status code. An http or https type should lead to documentation for humans. But clients should not fetch the type URI automatically. Absolute URIs are recommended.
card.example: Every out-of-credit error has type https://example.com/probs/out-of-credit. The app checks this type, not the title text, to start a credit top-up.

review.question: What does a missing type member mean?
review.answer: Its value is about:blank: the problem means no more than the HTTP status code.

screens.text: A problem type can add its own members. These are called extensions. They carry extra data, like balance 30 in the out-of-credit example of RFC 9457.
Clients must ignore any extensions that they do not recognize. This lets problem types evolve. A new member does not break a client that does not know it.

Clients should not parse the detail text for data. Extensions are the better way to give structured data. Example: a validation error adds an errors list. Each entry has a detail and a pointer to the bad field.

catch.question: A client gets a problem details object with a member it does not know. What must it do?
choices: Show the member as the error title
catch.explanation: Clients must ignore extensions they do not recognize. This lets problem types grow later.

card.text: A problem type can add its own members, called extensions. They carry extra data about that problem. Clients must ignore extensions they do not recognize. So problem types can add information later without breaking clients. Clients should not parse the detail text for data. Extensions are better for that, with fewer errors.
card.example: The out-of-credit problem adds balance: 30 and a list of accounts with top-up links. A validation error adds an errors list, each with a detail and a pointer like #/age.

review.question: Should a client read machine data from the detail text or from extensions?
review.answer: From extensions. Clients should not parse the detail text.

screens.text: Error details can leak information. This can help attackers, or expose the privacy of users. RFC 9457 says to vet the information in problem details.

RFC 9457 encourages you to avoid making implementation details, such as a stack dump, available through the HTTP interface. Problem details are not a tool to debug the implementation. They expose the HTTP interface.

The detail member should help the client correct the problem, not give debugging information. Example: after a database failure, send the title Purchase failed. Keep the SQL error and the stack trace out.

catch.question: What should a problem details response not show to the client?
choices: A stack dump of the server
A short title of the problem
A link to documentation for the problem type
catch.explanation: RFC 9457 warns against showing implementation details, like a stack dump, through the HTTP interface.

card.text: Error details can leak information. Attackers can use it to break into the system, or to harm the privacy of users. So check what each problem includes. RFC 9457 encourages you to avoid showing implementation details, like a stack dump, through the HTTP interface. Problem details are not a tool to debug the server. They describe the HTTP interface. The detail text should help the client fix the problem.
card.example: A database error breaks a purchase. The response has title Purchase failed and a detail that tells the client to try again later. The SQL error and the stack trace are not in it.

review.question: What should the detail member focus on?
review.answer: Helping the client correct the problem, not debugging information.

screens.text: Some REST services are not public. Only known callers may use them. So the service must check who is calling and what they may do.
Sign-in is central. One Identity Provider checks the user and issues an access token. The caller sends this token to the API.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  User --> IdP[Identity Provider]
  IdP --> Token[Access token]
  Token --> Endpoint[API endpoint]

screens.text: Then each endpoint makes its own access decision with the token. One check at sign-in is not enough. Example: a JWT arrives with aud set to another service. The orders endpoint rejects it.

catch.question: Where must a non-public REST service perform access control?
catch.explanation: OWASP says non-public REST services must perform access control at each API endpoint.

card.text: Non-public REST services must check access at each API endpoint. User sign-in should be central, at an Identity Provider that issues access tokens. Each endpoint then makes its own access decision with the token. Many APIs use JSON Web Tokens. Make sure a JWT has a signature or a MAC, and never accept alg none. By default, also check the claims iss, aud and exp.
card.example: A JWT arrives with aud set to another service. The orders endpoint rejects it, because the orders service is not in the token's audience.

review.question: Which three JWT claims should an API check by default?
review.answer: iss, the issuer; aud, the audience; and exp, the expiration time.

workedExample.problem: Your internal orders API accepts any request that comes from the company network.
steps: OWASP says non-public REST services must check access at each endpoint.
Users sign in at one Identity Provider, which issues access tokens.
Each endpoint checks the token and decides if this caller may do this operation.
workedExample.answer: Check an access token at every endpoint, instead of trusting the network.

tradeOff.situation: Your internal orders API runs inside the company network. A teammate wants to skip token checks on it, because only staff can reach it.
options: Trust the company network and skip token checks
Check an access token at each endpoint
Check a token only at sign-in and trust later calls

reasons.text: A REST service that is not public has to do access control at each of its endpoints.
The network is a strong wall here, and staff are the only people who can reach it.
Once sign-in checks the token, the later calls come from the same trusted user session.

tradeOff.explanation: OWASP says each endpoint makes its own access decision with the token. The cost is one token check on every call.

decisionCards.situation: A JWT arrives at the orders endpoint with aud set to another service. Its signature is valid.
options: Reject it, because the orders service is not in the audience
Accept it, because the signature is valid

reasons.text: A valid signature proves the token is real, and that is the main thing to check.
The aud claim is for the sign-in server, so the orders service can skip it.
By default, the API should require the iss, aud and exp claims and validate them.

decisionCards.explanation: OWASP says to require and validate iss, aud and exp by default, so a wrong audience is rejected. That is one more check on each request, but a token for another service cannot get in.

screens.text: A request travels over a network. It can carry a password, an API key or a JSON Web Token. These are credentials, and they must stay secret.
A secure REST service must only provide HTTPS endpoints. HTTPS protects credentials in transit. It also lets clients authenticate the service, and it guarantees the integrity of the data sent.

Example: a mobile app sends an access token with each call. Over HTTPS, the token is protected in transit. For highly privileged services, consider client certificates, so both sides authenticate each other.

source.title: OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet: HTTPS

catch.question: Why must a secure REST service offer only HTTPS endpoints?
choices: HTTPS responses are easier to cache
It protects credentials, like API keys, in transit
It removes the need for authentication
It lets the browser skip CORS checks
catch.explanation: HTTPS protects credentials in transit, lets clients authenticate the service, and protects the integrity of the data.

card.text: Secure REST services must only provide HTTPS endpoints. HTTPS protects credentials in transit, like passwords, API keys or JSON Web Tokens. It also lets clients authenticate the service. And it guarantees the integrity of the data sent. For highly privileged services, consider client certificates, so both sides authenticate each other.
card.example: A mobile app sends an access token with each call. Over HTTPS, the token is protected in transit, and the app knows it talks to the real service.

source.title: OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet: HTTPS

review.question: Name two things HTTPS gives a REST API.
review.answer: It protects credentials in transit, and clients can authenticate the service. It also protects data integrity.

screens.text: A URL can end up in a file. Web server logs can capture URLs. Logs are valuable to attackers, so a secret in a URL can leak.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Client[Client sends URL with key] --> Server[Web server]
  Server --> Log[Log keeps the URL and the key]

screens.text: So passwords, security tokens and API keys must not appear in the URL. In a GET request, send them in an HTTP header. In POST and PUT requests, use the body or a header.
Not OK: GET /orders/123?apiKey=a53f435643de32. The key is in the URL, so the log can keep it. OK: GET /orders/123, with the key in a header.

source.title: OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet: Sensitive information in HTTP requests

catch.question: Which request leaks the API key into web server logs?
choices: GET /orders/123 with the key in an HTTP header
POST /orders with the key in the request body
PUT /orders/123 with the key in an HTTP header
catch.explanation: Web server logs can capture URLs. So keys, tokens and passwords must not appear in the URL.

card.text: Passwords, security tokens and API keys should not appear in the URL. Web server logs can capture URLs, and that makes the logs valuable to attackers. In POST and PUT requests, send sensitive data in the request body or in headers. In GET requests, send sensitive data in an HTTP header.
card.example: Not OK: https://example.com/controller/123/action?apiKey=a53f435643de32. OK: https://example.com/resourceCollection/123/action, with the key in a header.

source.title: OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet: Sensitive information in HTTP requests

review.question: In a GET request, where should an API key go?
review.answer: In an HTTP header, never in the URL.

screens.text: 401 Unauthorized means the request lacks valid authentication credentials. The server must send a WWW-Authenticate header. The client may try again with new credentials.
403 Forbidden means the server understood the request but refuses it. If credentials were sent, they are not enough for access. The client should not repeat the request with the same credentials.
Example: a request with an expired token gets 401 and a WWW-Authenticate header. A signed-in user who asks for another team's report gets 403.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  User->>API: GET /reports/42 with a valid token
  API-->>User: 403 Forbidden

catch.question: A request has a valid token, but this user may not see the report. Which status code fits?
catch.explanation: 403 means the server understood the request but refuses it. The credentials are not enough for this resource.

card.text: 401 Unauthorized means the request lacks valid authentication credentials. The server must send a WWW-Authenticate header with at least one challenge. The client may try again with new credentials. 403 Forbidden means the server understood the request but refuses it. If credentials were sent, they are not enough for access. The client should not repeat the request automatically with the same credentials.
card.example: A request with an expired token gets 401 Unauthorized and a WWW-Authenticate header. A signed-in user who asks for another team's report gets 403 Forbidden.

review.question: Which of the two codes must come with a WWW-Authenticate header?
review.answer: 401 Unauthorized.

screens.text: A server may want to limit how many requests a user sends in a given amount of time. This is called rate limiting.
When a user goes over the limit, the server answers with status 429 Too Many Requests. The response should explain the condition. It may include a Retry-After header that says how long to wait.
Example: a site allows 50 requests per hour for each logged-in user. The next request gets 429 with Retry-After: 3600. A cache must not store a 429 response.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Site: request number 51 in one hour
  Site-->>Client: 429 Too Many Requests and Retry-After 3600

catch.question: Which status code says the client sent too many requests in a given amount of time?
catch.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests is the status code for rate limiting.

card.text: 429 Too Many Requests means the user sent too many requests in a given amount of time. This is rate limiting. The response should explain the condition. It may include a Retry-After header that says how long to wait. RFC 6585 does not say how the server counts requests. It can count per resource, across the server, or across many servers. A cache must not store a 429 response.
card.example: A site allows 50 requests per hour for each logged-in user. The next request gets 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After: 3600.

review.question: May a cache store a 429 response?
review.answer: No. A response with the 429 status code must not be stored by a cache.

workedExample.problem: One partner's script calls your API in a tight loop. The answers for all other partners get slow.
steps: Set a limit of requests per time for each client.
When a client goes over it, answer 429 Too Many Requests.
Add Retry-After if you can, so the script knows how long to wait.
workedExample.answer: Answer 429 when one client goes over its limit, and add Retry-After, so the script slows down.

tradeOff.situation: One partner's script calls your API in a tight loop. You want to stop this client without hurting other partners.
options: Answer 429 with Retry-After when this partner goes over its limit
Answer 503 Service Unavailable to every partner when load is high
Answer 403 Forbidden to this partner for every later request

reasons.text: 403 Forbidden stops the tight loop at once, and the partner can ask our team to unblock it.
429 means too many requests in a given time, and Retry-After tells the client how long to wait.
A 503 under high load protects the server, and it treats the partners in the same way.

tradeOff.explanation: 429 tells this one client it sent too many requests, and Retry-After tells it when to try again. The cost is that you must decide how to count requests for each client.

decisionCards.situation: Your API sends 429 responses with Retry-After. A teammate wants a shared cache to store them for a minute.
options: Let the cache store the 429 response
Do not let any cache store it

reasons.text: Caches are not allowed to store a response that has status code 429.
Retry-After tells a shared cache how long the 429 response stays valid for.
A stored 429 takes load off the server while the client waits out its limit.

decisionCards.explanation: RFC 6585 says a response with the 429 status code must not be stored by a cache. So the server answers each of these requests itself.

screens.text: A public REST service with no access control can be used too much by others. This can lead to big bills for bandwidth or compute. API keys reduce this risk.
So require an API key for every request to a protected endpoint. Revoke the key if the client breaks the usage agreement. Do not rely only on API keys for sensitive or high-value resources.
If requests with one key come in too quickly, return 429 Too Many Requests. Example: a free-plan key sends 100 requests per second. The API answers 429.

source.title: OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet: API keys

catch.question: Requests with one API key come in too quickly. Which status code does OWASP say to return?
catch.explanation: OWASP says to return 429 Too Many Requests if requests are coming in too quickly.

card.text: Public REST services with no access control can be farmed, which leads to big bills for bandwidth or compute. API keys reduce this risk. Require an API key for every request to a protected endpoint. Return 429 Too Many Requests if requests come in too quickly. Revoke the key if the client breaks the usage agreement. Do not rely only on API keys for sensitive or high-value resources.
card.example: A free-plan key sends 100 requests per second. The API answers 429 Too Many Requests. The client keeps breaking the usage agreement, so the provider revokes the key.

source.title: OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet: API keys

review.question: What should you do with an API key whose client breaks the usage agreement?
review.answer: Revoke the key.

screens.text: A server can ask the client to wait before it tries again. It does this with the Retry-After header. The value is an HTTP date or a number of seconds.
A number is a delay in seconds. Retry-After: 120 means wait 2 minutes before the next request. It is a delay, not a number of retries.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Server: request
  Server-->>Client: 503 and Retry-After 120
  Note over Client: wait 2 minutes

screens.text: A date also works. Retry-After: Fri, 31 Dec 1999 23:59:59 GMT means wait until that time. With 503, it says how long the service is expected to be unavailable.

catch.question: What does the response header Retry-After: 120 mean?
choices: The response stays fresh for 120 seconds
Wait 2 minutes before the next request
The connection stays open for 120 seconds
catch.explanation: A number in Retry-After is a delay in seconds. 120 seconds is 2 minutes.

card.text: Servers send Retry-After to say how long the client ought to wait before a follow-up request. The value is an HTTP date or a number of seconds. With 503 Service Unavailable, it says how long the service will be unavailable. With a 3xx redirect, it is the minimum wait before the redirected request.
card.example: Retry-After: 120 means wait 2 minutes. Retry-After: Fri, 31 Dec 1999 23:59:59 GMT means wait until that time.

review.question: What two forms can a Retry-After value have?
review.answer: An HTTP date, or a number of seconds to wait.

screens.text: The Claude API uses the token bucket algorithm for rate limiting. This describes how your capacity comes back after you use it.
Your capacity is continuously replenished, up to your maximum limit. It is not reset at fixed intervals. So it does not jump back to full at the start of each minute.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Use[Requests use capacity] --> Left[Capacity left]
  Time[Time passes] --> Left
  Left --> Max[Never above the maximum]

screens.text: Limits can also apply over shorter times. A rate of 60 requests per minute might be enforced as 1 request per second. So a short burst of requests can trigger rate limit errors.

catch.question: The Claude API uses the token bucket algorithm for rate limits. What does that mean for your capacity?
choices: It resets to full at the start of each minute
It refills all the time, up to your maximum limit
It refills only when you pay
catch.explanation: With a token bucket, capacity is replenished all the time up to the maximum, not reset at fixed times.

card.text: The Claude API uses the token bucket algorithm for rate limiting. Your capacity refills all the time, up to your maximum limit. It does not reset at fixed intervals. Limits can also apply over shorter times. For example, 60 requests per minute may be enforced as 1 request per second. So short bursts of requests can trigger rate limit errors.
card.example: A job has a limit of 60 requests per minute. It sends 20 requests in the same second. Some get 429 errors, because the limit can work like 1 request per second.

review.question: Why can a burst of requests get 429 errors under a per-minute limit?
review.answer: Limits can apply over shorter times, for example 60 per minute as 1 per second.

screens.text: A list operation returns an object with a top-level array of resources. The array is usually named value. If the list can ever grow very large, support paging from the start.
Each page has a nextLink field with an absolute URL for the next page. The client calls GET on that URL. The last page has no nextLink at all.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Page1[Page one with nextLink] --> Page2[Page two with nextLink]
  Page2 --> Last[Last page with no nextLink]

screens.text: Example: GET /items returns value with Item 01 to Item 99, and a nextLink. Adding paging later is a breaking change. Avoid a count of all items, because it can be expensive.

catch.question: In the Azure guidelines, how does a list response tell the client that another page exists?
choices: A hasMore field set to true
A nextLink field with an absolute URL
catch.explanation: Each page has a nextLink with an absolute URL for the next page. The last page has no nextLink.

card.text: A list operation returns an object with a top-level array of resources, usually named value. Support paging from the start if the list can ever grow very large. Adding paging later is a breaking change. Each page has a nextLink field with an absolute URL for the next page. Leave nextLink out on the last page, and never send it as null. Avoid a count of all items, because it can be expensive.
card.example: GET /items returns value with Item 01 to Item 99 and a nextLink. The client calls GET on the nextLink URL. The last page has no nextLink.

review.question: How does a client know it got the last page in an Azure-style API?
review.answer: The response has no nextLink field.

workedExample.problem: Your team designs GET /orders for a new API. The shop has only 300 orders today, so someone suggests no paging.
steps: Orders grow over time, so the list can become very large.
Adding paging later is a breaking change for clients.
So return a value array and a nextLink from the first version.
workedExample.answer: Add paging now, while there are no clients to break.

tradeOff.situation: Your team designs GET /orders for a new API. The shop has only 300 orders today, and a teammate says paging can wait.
options: Return all orders now and add paging in a later version
Return all orders with a count of all items instead of paging
Return value and nextLink from the first version

reasons.text: 300 orders fit easily in one response, so paging can wait until the shop really grows.
A total count lets clients plan their calls, so they can manage without paging.
If the list can grow very large, start paging early, since adding it later breaks clients.

tradeOff.explanation: Azure guidelines say to support paging if a list can grow large, since adding it later breaks clients. The cost is more work in version one.

decisionCards.situation: In an Azure-style API, you return the last page of a list. Your team debates how to show that no pages are left.
options: Return nextLink with the value null
Leave nextLink out of the response

reasons.text: A null nextLink is clear and explicit, so clients can test for it easily.
On the last page, nextLink is left out, not sent with a null value.
Some client libraries fail on a missing field, so an explicit null is safer.

decisionCards.explanation: Azure guidelines say to leave nextLink out on the last page, and never send it as null. Clients must be ready for a field that is missing.

screens.text: nextLink is an absolute URL. The client calls it with GET to get the next page. The service does any URL encoding that the URL needs.
nextLink must include every query parameter the service needs. This includes api-version. All pages use the same filter and sort order.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  First[First page] --> Link[nextLink with filter sort and api-version]
  Link --> Second[Second page]

screens.text: Example: GET /people?filter=name eq 'david'&orderby=hireDate returns a first page. Its nextLink keeps the same filter, sort order and api-version. Document that items may be skipped or duplicated across pages.

catch.question: Which query parameter must the nextLink URL include, according to the Azure guidelines?
choices: None, because the client adds them
catch.explanation: nextLink must include every query parameter the service needs, including api-version.

card.text: nextLink is an absolute URL that the client calls with GET to get the next page. The service does any URL encoding it needs. nextLink includes every query parameter the service needs, including api-version. All pages use the same filter and sort order. Document that items may be skipped or duplicated across pages. The exception is a service that takes special steps, like a snapshot that expires.
card.example: GET /people?filter=name eq 'david'&orderby=hireDate returns a first page. Its nextLink keeps the same filter, the same sort order and the api-version.

review.question: What must an Azure-style API document about items across pages?
review.answer: Items may be skipped or duplicated across pages, unless the service prevents it, for example with a snapshot.

screens.text: In Google APIs, the response has a next_page_token. The client sends it back as page_token to get the next page. An empty next_page_token is the only sign of the end.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>API: ListBooks
  API-->>Client: 50 books and next_page_token
  Client->>API: ListBooks with page_token

screens.text: Page tokens must be opaque. If users can take a token apart, they will. Then your paging details become part of the API, and you cannot change them without breaking users.
Base-64 encoding alone is not enough. A page token never gives authorization. The API may expire old tokens after a reasonable time. Three days is a good rule of thumb.

catch.question: Why must page tokens be opaque?
choices: So users cannot depend on how they work, and you can change it later
So they are shorter than page numbers
catch.explanation: If users can take tokens apart, they will. Then the paging details become part of the API and cannot change.

card.text: In Google APIs, the response has a next_page_token. The client sends it as page_token to get the next page. An empty next_page_token is the only sign of the end of the list. Page tokens must be opaque. If users can take them apart, they will, and then you cannot change your paging without breaking them. Base-64 encoding alone is not enough. A page token never gives authorization.
card.example: ListBooks returns 50 books and a next_page_token. The client sends it as page_token, with the same other parameters. The API may expire old tokens, and three days is a good rule of thumb.

review.question: How does a Google API say that the list has ended?
review.answer: next_page_token is empty. This is the only way.

screens.text: page_size sets the maximum number of results in one page. It must not be required. If the client leaves it out or sends 0, the API uses a default.
If page_size is above the maximum, the API should lower it to the maximum. Example: ListBooks has a maximum of 1000. A page_size of 5000 becomes 1000.
A negative value gets an INVALID_ARGUMENT error. The API may return fewer results than asked, even zero, before the end of the list. Only an empty next_page_token means the end.

catch.question: A client asks for page_size 5000, but the maximum is 1000. What should the API do?
choices: Turn off paging for this call
catch.explanation: If page_size is above the maximum, the API should lower it to the maximum.

card.text: page_size sets the maximum number of results in one page. It must not be required. If the client leaves it out or sends 0, the API uses a default, which it should document. If the value is above the maximum, the API should lower it to the maximum. A negative value gets an INVALID_ARGUMENT error. The API may return fewer results than asked, even zero, before the end of the list.
card.example: ListBooks has a default of 50 and a maximum of 1000. A page_size of 5000 becomes 1000. A page with 0 books but a next_page_token is not the end.

review.question: Does a short page mean that the list has ended?
review.answer: No. Only an empty next_page_token means the end.

screens.text: Two clients can change the same resource at the same time. The second save can wipe out the first one. This is data loss. A precondition on the request can stop it.
HTTP lets a client put a precondition on a request. Headers such as If-Match and If-None-Match set it. The server acts only if the resource is in the state the client expects.
A client reads a user with ETag 67ab43. It sends PUT with If-Match 67ab43. If someone changed the user in between, the server answers 412 Precondition Failed.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Server: PUT with If-Match 67ab43
  Server-->>Client: 412 Precondition Failed

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: Conditional requests

catch.question: What do headers like If-Match and If-None-Match let a client do?
choices: Choose the language of the response
Ask the server to compress the body
Set a precondition, so the server acts only if the resource is in the expected state
catch.explanation: These headers set a precondition for the request. They allow efficient caching and prevent data loss.

card.text: HTTP lets a client put a precondition on a request. The headers are If-Match, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Unmodified-Since and If-Range. They allow efficient caching. They also prevent data loss when clients update the same resource at the same time. A service must honor every precondition header it receives. ETags are strongly preferred over last-modified dates, because dates cannot tell apart updates less than a second apart.
card.example: A client reads a user with ETag "67ab43". It sends PUT with If-Match: "67ab43". If someone changed the user in between, the server answers 412 Precondition Failed.

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: Conditional requests

review.question: Why are ETags better than last-modified dates for preconditions?
review.answer: Dates cannot tell apart two updates made less than a second apart.

workedExample.problem: Two support agents edit the same customer at the same time. The second save silently removes the first agent's change.
steps: This is the lost update problem.
Return an ETag when a client reads the customer, as Azure says you should.
Honor If-Match with that ETag on each save, and answer 412 when it does not match.
workedExample.answer: Use ETags and If-Match, so a save based on old data fails with 412 instead of overwriting.

tradeOff.situation: Two support agents edit the same customer record in your API. The second save silently removes the first agent's change.
options: Return an ETag on read. On save, honor If-Match and answer 412 on a mismatch.
Let the last save win, and write both saves in a log.
Use the last-modified date as the precondition, because dates are simpler than ETags.

reasons.text: A stale save gets 412 and fails, so it cannot overwrite the other agent's change.
The log keeps both saves, so support can bring back a lost change if needed.
Last-modified dates do the same job as ETags, and they are easier to compare.

tradeOff.explanation: The ETag and If-Match make a stale save fail with 412 instead of overwriting. The cost is that clients must send the header and handle the 412 answer.

decisionCards.situation: Your service sends ETags. A client sends PUT with an If-Match value that is out of date.
options: Answer 412 Precondition Failed and do not apply the update.
Apply the update, because the client sent the whole resource.

reasons.text: The client sent the whole resource, so its PUT holds the full new state.
Precondition headers are mainly for caches, so a write API can skip them.
A server may not ignore a precondition header, because ignoring it can be unsafe.

decisionCards.explanation: A service must honor the precondition headers it receives. The client then reads the resource again before it can save.

screens.text: A client sends an update. The update works, but the reply is lost. The client does not know this, so it sends the identical update again.
With a version number as the ETag, this retry is treated as a conflict. The update did work, but the retry looks like a clash.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Server: Update with version ETag
  Server-->>Client: Reply is lost
  Client->>Server: Same update again
  Server-->>Client: Conflict

screens.text: So Azure says to use a hash of the representation of the resource, not a version number. Weak ETags are allowed if you need to tell meaningful changes from cosmetic ones.

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: Computing ETags

catch.question: Why do the Azure guidelines prefer a hash of the resource over a version number as the ETag?
choices: With a version number, a retried update can be seen as a conflict
Clients cannot read a version number
catch.explanation: An update works, but its reply is lost. With a version number as the ETag, the identical retry can look like a conflict.

card.text: Azure says you should return an ETag with any operation that returns or updates a resource. A version number is a natural ETag for versioned resources.
